en: The essential commentary on the *Triṃśikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* is the same [as previously stated].
Alternatively, some maintain that there are no mental factors (*caitta*) distinct from the mind (*citta*).

In order to refute these various divergent attachments and to enable them to attain a correct understanding of the profound and subtle principle of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), this treatise was composed.
Regarding the objects of reference, there are further two types:
the first clarifies the composition of the treatise,
and the latter reveals its transmission and translation.
Although the Buddha, the Bhagavan, has taught many dharma-gates to compassionately guide sentient beings, their essential points consist of four causal conditions:
consciousness-only, signlessness, suchness, and teaching in accordance with the faculties and dispositions of beings; these are each explained in various sutras.
Regarding the other three systems of reasoning, there have already been extensive treatises;
however, the profound meaning of Consciousness-Only (Vijñaptimātra) has not yet been clearly elucidated.
This was during the nine hundred years following the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha.
The Bodhisattva Asaṅga attended upon the Great Compassionate Honored One and requested him to expound the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Madhyāntavibhāga-śāstra*, and other treatises.
He himself composed the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Abhidharmasamuccaya) to elucidate the principle of Vijñaptimātra.
As it was not yet perfectly clear and luminous, I,
Vasubandhu— the Bodhisattva of Increasing Wisdom— thereupon composed two treatises to elucidate the One Vehicle.
The first of these is titled the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (The Twenty Verses on Consciousness-Only).
The first part elucidates the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) by refuting external doctrines and briefly presenting our own school’s tenets.
The subsequent section, titled *Triṃśikā-vijñapti*,
elucidates the principle of consciousness-only through thirty verses, briefly refuting external doctrines and extensively presenting our own school’s tenets.
Before he had yet composed a commentary on the *Abhidharmakośa* and attained contentment,
the ten great masters of the treatises, such as Dharmapāla and others, reached the ultimate excellence of their own school and thoroughly mastered the doctrines of outsiders;
their knowledge and vision became ever more expansive, bringing vast benefit and joy to many.
At that time, they admired his virtue and thus bestowed upon him the title "Bodhisattva.
Each composed a *śāstra* to proclaim and elucidate his verses.
Although these true teachings were both practiced in the world, [the latter eventually prevailed].
The Dharma-treasury had not yet spread from the Western Regions to the Eastern Land of China.
During the Zhenguan era of our Tang dynasty, there was a Great Tripitaka Master of Universal Enlightenment whose name was Xuanzang.
Having left home at a young age, his aspirations were loftier than those of the world.
His teachers were drawn from both near and far, and his mastery encompassed both internal and external disciplines.
Having thoroughly investigated and refined the principles of the Dharma throughout the Middle Kingdom, he attained complete penetration.
He resolved to investigate the traces of other teachings;
thereupon, he brushed off his robes for the lands of the East and took up his staff for the Western Heavens.
Wandering through the realms of the Way, he traveled extensively to seek out and examine the scriptures.
He exhausted the erroneous views of former sages and mastered what the virtuous of antiquity had not heard.
Once his reputation was established and his doctrine perfected, he returned to his native land.
His Majesty, the Former Emperor of our Tang dynasty, invited him to serve as State Preceptor.
Although he translated great true sutras and extensively rendered authentic treatises,
the profound meaning of Vijñaptimātra remained as secret as a crest-jewel;
because the recipient was not yet the right person, he did not immediately transmit or translate it.
It was solely for the sake of his compassionate grace that he alone instructed upon this principle.
Initially, in the twenty-second year of the Zhenguan era, he translated this version of the verses at Cien Monastery;
later, toward the end of the Xianqing era, he translated the *Śāstra* at Yuhua Palace Monastery in Fangzhou.
At the time of the initial translation, ten commentaries circulated separately;
later, due to repeated requests for clarification, they were synthesized into a single volume,
which encompasses technical terminology and integrates both heterodox and orthodox views.
Now, adopting the correct principle, I shall explain the verses.
The discussion on the "object-condition" (*ālambana*) is concluded.
As for what is "accepted as the tenet," there is both a general and a specific sense.
In summary, the general analysis takes consciousness-only as its tenet; this is because,
based on consciousness-only, [phenomena] are neither existent nor non-existent.
Because this correct treatise is composed on the principle of non-apprehension;
if one clings to the existence of emptiness, one does not abide in consciousness-only,
for the mind that apprehends existence is mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
To explain it specifically:
the doctrine, reasoning, practice, and fruit of Consciousness-Only (Vijñaptimātra) are taken as the primary tenets.

This treatise was composed so that sentient beings, by relying on the teaching of Consciousness-Only, may awaken to the principle of Consciousness-Only, practice the conduct of Consciousness-Only, and attain the fruit of Consciousness-Only.
The teaching refers to the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, various Mahāyāna scriptures, and so forth;
the principle refers to dharmas such as the eight consciousnesses and the three natures;
and the practice refers to the wisdom of contemplation regarding the six perfections without signs.
The fruits refer to wisdom, abandonment, enlightenment, and nirvana.
These tenets will be examined in detail in the relevant passages.
This concludes the exposition of the tenets.
Regarding what is meant by "that to which one returns," according to various sutras and treatises, there are briefly three types:
namely, returning to the treasury (藏), returning to the vehicle (乘), and returning to the time (時).
"Piṭaka" refers to the two piṭakas:
those of the Bodhisattvas and the Śrāvakas.
Each of these two has three [divisions].
That is to say, the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma explain meditative concentration and wisdom according to their respective predominant characteristics.
"Vehicle" refers to the five vehicles:
namely, the unsurpassed vehicle, the solitary realizer vehicle, the śrāvaka vehicle, as well as the human and celestial vehicles.
"Time" refers to the three periods:
namely, the beginning, the middle, and the end.
At the beginning, it is taught that [all things] exist.
Next, it speaks only of emptiness;
later, it speaks of both that which is neither empty nor existent.
This treatise thus returns to the Abhidharma within the Bodhisattva-piṭaka.
It reveals the meaning of the Bodhisattva’s principles, practices, and fruits, thereby elucidating the training in wisdom;
within the five vehicles, it leads one to take refuge in the Unsurpassed Vehicle (Anuttarayāna),
as it demonstrates that there is no vehicle superior to this, whether in terms of the subject who rides or the object being ridden.
Within the three periods, one returns to the third period,
because it clearly expounds that the principles of existence and emptiness are ultimately perfected.
This concludes the clarification of what is returned to.
Next, the established [treatise] is explained.
This consists of two parts:
first, the explanation of the title.
Next, the commentary explains the verses.
Regarding the explanation of the title, as stated in the *Śāstra* itself:
"The name of this root treatise is the *Triṃśikā-vijñaptimātratā* (Thirty Verses on Consciousness-Only)."
The principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) is rendered complete by these thirty verses, neither more nor less;
this is because it is named according to its number of verses, just as the *Śata-śāstra-vyākhyāna* and other works are titled based on their respective verse counts.
It merely negates external objects to reveal that they do not exist,
and it expresses the internal mind to reveal that it does not fail to exist.
Because it is neither existent nor non-existent, it is called "consciousness-only" (vijñaptimātra).
It is called a "treatise" (*śāstra*) because it explains, distinguishes, and definitively resolves [the meaning].
It explains and distinguishes the meaning of the nature and characteristics of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*), and definitively resolves the meanings of reality and error.
The explanation of the title is thus completed.
Regarding the explanation of the treatise:
according to various treatises, it generally possesses three parts:
the homage, the statement of intent, and the main body of the work.
The body of the treatise is now formally presented,
followed by the conclusion and the dedication of merit;
whether these opening and closing sections are included depends on the author’s intention.
This treatise consists solely of the main body of the doctrine.
Within this, it is largely divided into three sections.
The first one and a half verses provide a brief exposition of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
Next, twenty-three and a half verses extensively explain consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
Following this, five verses clarify the stages of spiritual practice (*bhāvanāvasthā*).
Regarding the first, which briefly explains the origin of the treatise, it says:
If there is only consciousness, why do the world and the various holy teachings speak of a self and dharmas?
The verse says:
"By means of metaphorical designation, the self and dharmas are spoken of; they manifest in various forms."
That [object] depends on what is transformed by consciousness; this transforming [consciousness] is of only three kinds:
namely, the ripening, the deliberating, and the consciousness that discriminates objects.
Commentary:
The verse consists of six lines, which are divided into two meanings.
The first three lines explain the objection and establish the thesis;
the latter three lines set forth the names of the transformative [consciousnesses].
Within the preceding section, there are again two parts:
the first two lines resolve external objections,
while the middle three lines state the thesis and provide the formal explanation.
The worldly teachings speak of a self and phenomena;
however, these exist only as provisional designations and lack intrinsic reality.
"Self" refers to a sovereign agent.
Dharma means that which serves as a guide and sustains;
both of these possess various modes of manifestation,
such as the various modes of the self.
This refers to the various characteristics of phenomena, such as sentient beings, living entities, stream-enterers, once-returners, and so forth;
and the various aspects of reality,
such as substances, qualities, activities, the aggregates, the bases, and the elements.
"Transformation" refers to the appearance of difference as it is provisionally designated in accordance with conditions.
If these various characteristics are established by way of such provisional designation, upon what do they depend for their accomplishment?
Those characteristics are all provisionally designated based on the transformations of consciousness.
"Consciousness" means discernment. Herein,
consciousness also includes mental factors (*caitta*),
because they are associated with it in meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
"Transformation" refers to the substance of consciousness transforming so as to appear as two parts;
since both the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) arise based upon self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*),
it is in reliance upon these two parts that the self and dharmas are conventionally established.
Because those two [subject and object] have no basis apart from this,
although these characteristics of self and phenomena exist within internal consciousness,
they manifest as if they were external objects due to conceptual construction.
Since beginningless time, all classes of sentient beings have taken this as a real self and real phenomena due to their cognitive conditioning.
Just as one afflicted by a dream, by the power of that affliction,
the mind manifests appearing as the various marks of external objects.
Based on this, they grasp at external objects as being substantially existent.
However, the real self and real dharmas grasped by the ignorant do not exist at all;
they are merely designated in accordance with deluded sentiments, and are therefore said to be "provisional."
The internal consciousness transforms into appearances that resemble a self and resemble phenomena; although these exist, they do not possess the nature of a real self or real phenomena.
Nevertheless, because they appear as such, they are said to be "provisional.
Since external objects are established according to mental dispositions, they do not exist in the manner that consciousness does.
Since internal consciousness necessarily arises in dependence upon causes and conditions, it is not non-existent, unlike the [external] objects.
By this, the two attachments of superimposition and denial are refuted.
Because objects are provisionally established based on internal consciousness, they exist only conventionally.
Consciousness is also ultimately existent because it is the basis for the objects that are conventionally designated;
the following three phrases set forth the names of the "transforming" [consciousnesses],
which are indicated by the first phrase.
The remaining two lines are as follows:
Although the images transformed by consciousness are of infinite kinds,
the types of the transforming consciousnesses are only three.
The first refers to maturation (*vipāka*),
because the eighth consciousness is predominantly of the nature of maturation.
The second refers to deliberation (*manana*).
This is because the seventh consciousness constantly and thoroughly deliberates.
"Three" refers to the discernment of objects;
that is, because the objects discerned by the preceding six consciousnesses are coarse in their characteristics.
The word "and" (*ca*) indicates that the six consciousnesses together constitute a single category.
Regarding the statement that these three are all called "transforming consciousnesses" (*pariṇāma-vijñāna*),
there are two types of transforming consciousness.
The first is the causally transforming [consciousness].
This refers to the two types of causal latencies within the eighth consciousness: those of uniform outflow (*nisyanda*) and those of maturation (*vipāka*).
The latencies of uniform outflow are caused to grow by the perfuming of the seven consciousnesses through their wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral states.
The ripening habitual tendencies (vipāka-vāsanā) are caused to grow by the impure wholesome and unwholesome [karmas] within the six consciousnesses.
Regarding the second, the transformation into fruit:
this refers to the power of the aforementioned two kinds of habitual tendencies.
There are eight consciousnesses that arise, manifesting various appearances.
Because the habit-energies of similar outflows (*niṣyanda-vāsanā*) serve as their causal conditions,
the eight consciousnesses arise with distinct essential natures and characteristics.
It is called an outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) because the fruit resembles its cause.
The ripening habitual tendencies (*vipāka-vāsanā*), acting as a condition for growth, bring about the eighth consciousness.
Because it continuously compensates for the power of projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*),
it is designated by the name "maturation" (*vipāka*).
The first six consciousnesses, which are produced as compensation for completing karma (*paripūraka-karman*), arise from this maturation.
It is called "born of maturation" (vipākaja),
but it is not called "maturation" (vipāka) itself,
because it is subject to interruption.
That which is the prior maturation (*vipāka*) and that which is born of maturation (*vipākaja*) is called the "fruit of maturation" (*vipākaphala*),
because the fruit differs from its cause.

In this context, for the time being, the transforming consciousness (*pariṇāma-vijñāna*) that is the fruit— which is the storehouse (*ālaya*) where self-love clings and which maintains the seeds of defilement— is designated as "maturation."
This does not mean all [cases].
The initial brief exposition is concluded;
next follows the detailed exposition below.
Within this, there are three parts.
First, fourteen and a half verses distinguish the three transformations of consciousness.
Second, one verse reveals the meaning of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).
Thereafter, eight verses explain and resolve external objections.
The three transformative capacities are distinguished and divided into three parts.
First, what are the characteristics of the primary transformative capacity?
The verse says:
The first is the ālayavijñāna, Maturation, possessing all seeds,
Inconceivable, grasping, And the constant perception of place, together with contact.

Mental attention (*manasikāra*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*)—these associated [factors] are exclusively the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) and are non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*). Contact (*sparśa*) and the others are likewise;
they flow constantly like a torrential stream, until they are abandoned at the stage of the Arhat.
The commentary states:

These two and a half verses explain the first transformation (*pariṇāma*) by means of ten thematic gates. First, regarding the "ālayavijñāna," this refers to the gate of its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
This first transformation is called *ālaya* in the teachings of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
This consciousness possesses the meanings of "that which is stored" (ālaya) and "that which is clung to as a store" (ālīna).
This is because it serves as a mutual condition for the defilements,
and because sentient beings cling to it as their internal self.
This demonstrates all its specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*),
because it maintains cause and effect as its own characteristic.
Although the states (*avasthā*) of this consciousness's own characteristic are many, [it remains so].
The first fault among the [three] is the most serious;
therefore, it is specifically mentioned. To say "maturation" (*vipāka*) refers to the perspective of the characteristics of the fruit.
This is the wholesome and unwholesome karma that draws forth rebirth within the various realms and destinies.
It is called "maturation" (vipāka) because it is a maturation-result;
for apart from this, no other dharma can be found that is capable of universally upholding such a preeminent maturation-result.
Although the characteristics of this consciousness as a result exist in many states and many varieties, [it is designated by this name].
Because its maturation (*vipāka*) is broad and uncommon, it is described as "pervasive. "Containing all seeds" refers to the aspect of its causal characteristic.
It is called "containing all seeds" because it is able to maintain the seeds of all phenomena so that they are not lost.
Because apart from this, no other phenomenon can be found that is capable of universally maintaining the seeds of all phenomena.
In this context, what phenomenon is designated as a "seed"?
It refers to the specific functional capacity within the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) that directly produces its own result.
This [seed] is neither identical to nor different from the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) and its resulting effects;
for such is the principle governing essence and function, cause and effect.
Although the seed depends upon the substance of the eighth consciousness, it is not distinct from it.
However, it is the *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect) of this very consciousness,
and not that of others, because its *darśanabhāga* (subjective aspect) constantly takes this as its object.
Since all contaminated seeds are non-distinct in substance from the retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), they are subsumed under the category of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Because both cause and effect are of a virtuous nature (*kuśala*), they are also termed "virtuous" and so forth.
Since the various untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) are not subsumed under the nature of the retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*),
and because both cause and effect are subsumed under the category of virtue, they are designated solely as "virtuous" and so forth.
Because it is able to maintain these seeds, it is called "all-seeded" (*sarvabījaka*);
this constitutes its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Although there are many types of causal characteristics (*nimitta*) for this consciousness, its maintenance of seeds is unique (*asādhāraṇa*).
Therefore, it is explained partially that the object-condition (*ālambana*) consists of the apprehension of the place of appropriation (*upādāna*) which is unknowable.
Herein, "apprehension" (*vijñapti*) refers to the function of the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) to have cognitive discernment with respect to its own object-condition.
Discernment (*vijñapti*) is the mode of activity (*ākāra*) of consciousness.
Since consciousness has discernment as its mode of activity,
this function of discernment is subsumed under the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*).
That which is called "abode" refers to the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*),
for it is the locus upon which all these sentient beings depend.
This means that due to the maturing power of the seeds of common characteristics,
the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) transforms into the appearance of the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*), such as form and so forth;
that is, the external primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*).
Although the transformations produced by each sentient being are distinct,
they are similar in appearance and do not differ in location,
just as the light from many lamps pervades everywhere and appears as one.
There are two types of appropriation:
namely, the various seeds and the body with its sense faculties.
Regarding the various seeds:
This refers to the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of conceptualization regarding various marks and names;
that is, all seeds of contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) sustained by the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).
Because this consciousness subsumes their nature, they are its objects of perception (*ālambana*).
Although the seeds of untainted dharmas depend upon this consciousness,
because they are not subsumed under its nature, they are not its objects; yet,
although they are not its objects, they are not separate from it.
Just as the nature of suchness does not contradict vijñapti-mātra,
the "body with faculties" refers to the various material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*) and their physical bases (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
By the power of the maturation of the uncommon seeds of the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*),
it transforms into what appear as the sense organs (*indriya*) and their physical bases (*adhiṣṭhāna*),
namely, the internal primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*).
Because of the power of the maturation of seeds with common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-bīja*),
[the mind] also transforms into the likeness of those [objects] within the locus of another's body;
otherwise, there would be no sense of experiencing the objects of others.
These seeds and the body with its sense organs are both objects of perception.
By the power of causes and conditions, when the ālayavijñāna arises in its own essence,
it internally transforms itself into seeds and the body with its sense organs.
The external world transforms into the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*).
This is because [the consciousness] arises by depending upon that which has been transformed as its own objective referent (*ālambana*) and mode of activity (*ākāra*). Regarding "incognizable":
this refers to the fact that this mode of activity is extremely subtle and thus difficult to discern.
Alternatively, because the internally grasped objects of this [consciousness] are also subtle,
and because the external receptacle world is difficult to fathom,
it is called "unknowable. That which is always associated with contact, attention, feeling, perception, and volition refers to the gate of association with mental factors (*caitta*).
From beginningless time until it has not yet been transformed,
the ālayavijñāna is at all stages constantly associated with these five mental factors,
because they are subsumed under the category of universal mental factors (sarvatraga-caitta).
The characteristics of these universal mental factors will be explained in detail later.
Although these five factors, such as contact (*sparśa*), differ from the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) in their modes of activity (*ākāra*),
they are termed "associated" (*samprayukta*) because they share the same time, basis (*āśraya*), object (*ālambana*), substance (*vastu*), and so forth.
As for the five object-specific mental factors being dissociated [from this consciousness],
it is because desire— which aspires toward desired objects—
is absent in this consciousness, which functions spontaneously without aspiration.
Resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) maintains a determined object;
because this consciousness is dull and lacks such maintenance, it does not do so.
Mindfulness (*smṛti*) merely clearly records objects previously experienced.
This consciousness is dull and weak, unable to clearly remember;
it can, however, cause the mind to focus single-pointedly on an object.
This consciousness functions spontaneously, perceiving objects moment by moment.
Wisdom (*prajñā*) functions solely to discern qualities and so forth;
because this consciousness is subtle and indistinct, it cannot perform such discernment.
Therefore, it does not associate with the specific object-conditions (*viṣaya-niyata-viṣayālambana*).
Because this consciousness is exclusively of the nature of maturation (vipāka),
it is not associated with anything wholesome, defiled, or the like.
As for the four types of indeterminate states, such as regret (kaukṛtya) and so forth—

Because it is interrupted, it is certainly not a maturation (*vipāka*). That it is associated with only neutral feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*) is because the word "associated" (*saṃprayukta*) is stated in both places [in the sūtra].
Furthermore, the mode of activity (*ākāra*) of this consciousness is extremely obscure.
Because it cannot discern the characteristics of favorable or unfavorable objects,
it is associated exclusively with the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
Furthermore, the feeling associated with this [state] is solely maturation (*vipāka*).
It proceeds according to the momentum of prior projecting karma without depending on present conditions;
because it proceeds solely by the force of the power of wholesome or unwholesome karma,
it is exclusively a neutral feeling (upekṣā-vedanā).
The two feelings of suffering and pleasure are born of maturation,
yet they are not true maturations,
because they depend upon present conditions.
It is not associated with these [mental factors].
Furthermore, because this consciousness is never transformed,
sentient beings constantly grasp it as their internal self.
If it were associated with the two feelings of pleasure and pain, it would undergo transformation;
how then could it be clung to as a self?

Therefore, it is always associated with the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*). This [statement] regarding its being "unobscured and neutral" (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) is from the perspective of the classification by way of the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*).
There are four kinds of dharmas:
namely, wholesome, unwholesome, obscured-neutral, and unobscured-neutral.
This consciousness is exclusively unobscured-neutral because its nature is that of maturation (*vipāka*).
If the ripening consciousness were either wholesome or defiled,
the processes of saṃsāra and its cessation would be impossible to establish.
Furthermore, this consciousness serves as the basis for both the wholesome and the defiled.
Furthermore, because the wholesome and the defiled are mutually contradictory,
this consciousness should not serve as the support for both;
moreover, this consciousness is by nature that which is perfumed (*bhāvyatva*).
If it were wholesome or defiled, then—as with an extremely fragrant scent—it should not be susceptible to perfuming;
since there would be nothing to be perfumed, both the causes and effects of defilement and purity would fail to be established.
Therefore, this is exclusively non-obscured neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Obscuration (*nivṛti*) refers to defiled phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*).
It is so called because it obstructs the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) and because it can veil the mind, causing it to be impure.
This consciousness is called "unobscured" because it is not defiled.
It is "defined" because it possesses fruits that are either desirable or undesirable, and because it can be specifically distinguished by its excellence and spontaneity.

Because this is neither wholesome nor unwholesome, it is called "indeterminate" (avyākṛta). The same applies to contact (*sparśa*) and the other [mental factors]. This is an analogy between the mental factors and the primary mind:

just as with contact and attention (*manasikāra*), the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is likewise indeterminate; its maturation, its object-condition (*ālambana*), and its mode-of-apprehension (*ākāra*) are all unknowable.
Because they take three kinds of objects, are associated with five factors, and are unobscured-neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*),
it is said that contact and the others are likewise;
this should be explained according to what is appropriate.
This does not mean everything [is the storehouse consciousness]. Otherwise,
just as "consciousness" is called "all-seeded," it would follow that contact and the other mental factors would receive perfuming and maintain seeds.

It should be understood that for each sentient being there are six kinds of entities. Regarding the gateway of the metaphor for the *pratītyasamutpāda* (dependent origination) as "constantly flowing like a torrent":
"constant" means that this consciousness, from beginningless time, has been a single, homogeneous continuum, eternally uninterrupted.
This is because it is the fundamental basis for the designation of realms, destinies, and births;

by its nature, it firmly maintains the seeds so that they are not lost. "Transformation" refers to this consciousness, which from beginningless time arises and ceases moment by moment, undergoing change and variation from one moment to the next.
Because the cause perishes while the fruit arises, they are neither eternal nor identical.
It may be said that this refers to the transformation of consciousness which perfumes seeds;
the term "constant" excludes interruption.
This indicates that [phenomena] are neither eternal nor discontinuous;
rather, like a violent torrent, the law of cause and effect is such that,
just as the flow of a rushing stream is neither severed nor permanent, yet continues for a long time, causing things to be carried away and submerged.
This consciousness is likewise:
from beginningless time, it has continued in a succession of arising and ceasing, being neither eternal nor annihilated;
it causes sentient beings to drift and drown, preventing them from attaining liberation.
Furthermore, just as a torrent, though struck by winds and other factors to produce various waves, continues its flow without interruption,
so too is this consciousness:
although it encounters various conditions to give rise to visual and other sensory cognitions, it remains in constant succession.
Furthermore, just as a violent torrent carries along fish, grass, and other objects, drifting up and down without letting them go,
so too is this consciousness:
it perpetually evolves in a continuous stream together with internal habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and external factors such as contact (*sparśa*).
Through this analogy, the meaning is revealed that the cause and effect of this consciousness have been neither interrupted nor eternal since beginningless time.
That is to say, from time immemorial, the nature of this consciousness has seen the arising of effects and the cessation of causes moment by moment.
Because the fruit arises, it is not annihilation;
because the cause ceases, it is not eternal.
Since this non-annihilation and non-eternality is the principle of supreme arising, [it is the Middle Way].
It is said that this consciousness constantly evolves like a flowing stream.
Regarding the stage where it is abandoned at the level of an Arhat, this refers to the point when noble beings have completely and finally severed the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
He is named an Arhat.
At that time, because this consciousness is forever separated from the coarse tendencies of afflictions,
it is described as "equanimity."
The term "Arhat" mentioned here encompasses the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) across all three vehicles,
as they have all eternally destroyed the thieves of the afflictions and are worthy of receiving the sublime offerings of the world.
Because they will never again undergo birth in discrete segments;
because from the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*) upward, all afflictions (*kleśa*) no longer arise for Bodhisattvas;
and because they proceed spontaneously within the swift current of the Dharma.
Because one is able to initiate all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) within all conditioned phenomena,
and because they increase and intensify moment by moment,
this stage is designated as "non-retrogression from enlightenment."
However, with this consciousness as its object, the views of self, craving, and so forth no longer grasp it as their internal self.
This stage may also be designated as that of an Arhat;
by virtue of this, the name "ālayavijñāna" is forever lost.
However, because the Arhat has completely and utterly exhausted the afflictive latencies (*dausthulya*) within this consciousness,
it no longer clings to it as an internal self; thus,
it permanently loses this designation.
This is explained as "abandonment," but it does not mean abandoning the entire substance of the eighth consciousness; otherwise,
Arhats would lack a consciousness to sustain their seeds.
At that time, he entered *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
Although the eighth consciousness is fully possessed by all sentient beings,
it is established under various names according to its different functions.
That is to say, it is called "mind" (citta) because it is accumulated by the seeds perfumed by various phenomena;
or it is called "Arhat."
Because it maintains the seeds and the various material sense-faculties so that they are not relinquished,
it is called the "basis of the knowable" (*jñeyāśraya*),
as it serves as the support for all dharmas that are known, whether defiled or pure.
It is also called the seed-consciousness (*bīja-vijñāna*),
because it is able to universally sustain all seeds of both the mundane and supramundane realms.
These various names apply throughout all stages.
It is also called the *ālaya*,
because it stores and preserves all factors belonging to the category of defilement so that they are not lost,
and because it is grasped as one's own internal self by means of self-view, self-love, and so forth.
This name applies only to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and those in training (*śaikṣa*);

it does not apply to those in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) or non-retrogressive bodhisattvas, because for them there is no sense of being a storehouse (*ālaya*) that clings to defiled phenomena.
Alternatively, it is called the "maturation consciousness" (*vipākavijñāna*).
Because it can induce the maturation of the fruits of karma— whether wholesome or unwholesome— that leads to birth and death,
this designation applies only to the stages of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), and various bodhisattvas;
it does not apply to the stage of a Tathāgata.
Because it possesses dharmas that are maturation-born and indeterminate,
it is called the "stainless consciousness" (*amala-vijñāna*),
as it is the true substratum for all most extremely pure, untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas.
This name exists only in the stage of the Tathāgata.
This is because Bodhisattvas and followers of the Two Vehicles possess tainted seeds that are susceptible to perfuming, and have not yet attained the thoroughly purified eighth consciousness.
The name *ālaya* is used because its faults are grave and because it is the first to be abandoned; herein,
the term specifically refers to the substance of the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).
The Bodhisattva relinquishes it when he is about to attain enlightenment;
the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas relinquish it upon entering the nirvāṇa without remainder.
The essence of the immaculate consciousness (amala-vijñāna) has no time of relinquishment, because its benefit and happiness for sentient beings are inexhaustible.
However, the eighth consciousness generally comprises two states:
first, the state with outflows (sāsrava),
which is subsumed under the category of the indeterminate (avyākṛta).
It is associated only with the five factors beginning with contact (*sparśa*),
and takes as its object only the previously mentioned appropriated bases (*ātmabhāvādhiṣṭhāna*).
Second, the two untainted states (*anāsrava-avasthā*).
It is comprised solely of the nature of goodness and is associated with twenty-one mental factors;
namely, five each from the universal and the object-specific categories.
The eleven wholesome [mental factors] are always associated with all minds,
because they constantly delight in realizing and knowing the objects under observation.
Because he constantly maintains mental attention toward the objects of observation;
because he constantly and clearly remembers objects previously experienced;
and because the Blessed One possesses no state of mind that is not concentrated.
Because it constantly discerns all phenomena;
because it is always associated with supreme pure faith and so forth;
and because it is free from defilement.
Because it is free from distraction,
this [state] is also associated exclusively with the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*),
as it functions spontaneously and perpetually in a state of equilibrium.
All phenomena (*sarvadharma*) serve as its objective referents (*ālambana*),
because the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) universally takes all phenomena as its objects.
Thus has been explained the characteristic of the first transformation.
What are the characteristics of the second transformative consciousness?
The verse says:
Next is the second transformative consciousness; this consciousness is named *manas*.
Depending on that [manas] and taking it as its object, it has the nature and characteristic of cogitation;
four afflictions are always associated with it— namely, self-delusion,
self-view, self-love, and self-pride— as well as others such as contact.
It is comprised within the obscured-unspecified (nivṛtāvyākṛta). It is bound according to where it arises.
For an Arhat, it does not exist in the meditative attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) or in the supramundane path (lokottaramārga).
Thus is the explanation.
These three verses are divided into two parts:
first, the manifestation of the sequence;
second, the explanation of the characteristics of consciousness. Next, regarding the "second transformation," this reveals its sequence.
Therefore, the commentary states:
"Next, after the first type of consciousness that transforms through maturation (vipāka-vijñāna),
one should explain the characteristics of the consciousness that transforms through volition (manana-vijñāna)."
The following ten sections provide an analysis of the characteristics of consciousness. First, regarding the etymological definition:
this consciousness is specifically termed *manas* in the sacred teachings because it excels other consciousnesses in its constant and thorough deliberation (*santīraṇa*).
How does this name differ from that of the sixth consciousness?
This is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound,
just like the name "storehouse consciousness" (*ālayavijñāna*).
Since consciousness is identical to the mind,
it is a *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound,
just as in the term "eye-consciousness" (*cakṣurvijñāna*).
Because consciousness (*vijñāna*) is distinct from the mind (*manas*),
yet fearing that this [consciousness] might be confused with that [mind],
the various holy teachings refer to the seventh [consciousness] merely by the name "mind."
Furthermore, it is designated as "mind" (*manas*) to distinguish it from consciousness (*vijñāna*), because it is inferior to other forms of consciousness in its accumulation and discernment;
or, it is called simply "mind" to show that it serves as the immediate support for that mental consciousness. That upon which it depends refers to the second support.
This refers to the aforementioned first transformative consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
Since the Noble Ones state that this consciousness relies upon the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*),
it can only arise when the seeds of consciousness and its manifest consciousness serve as simultaneous supports (*sahabhū-āśraya*).
Although there is no interruption, there is transformation,
because [a state] must have a basis in order to arise.
"Transformation" refers to the process of saṃsāric flow.
This demonstrates that this consciousness constantly relies upon that [underlying] consciousness to apprehend its objects.
Herein, the three meanings of "basis" (*āśraya*) should be clarified;
however, fearing prolixity, they are not recorded here.
The *Śatadharma-śāstra-vyākhyā* clarifies: "That which takes that as its object" refers to the third [of the four] objects of cognition (*ālambana*).

"That" refers to the aforementioned consciousness which serves as its support (*āśraya*), for the Noble Ones have taught that this consciousness takes the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) as its object.
One takes only the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect) of the *ālaya-vijñāna* as the self;

one does not take the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect), the seeds within consciousness, or the associated mental factors (*samprayukta-dharma*) as "mine," because the grasping for self and the grasping for "mine" do not arise simultaneously.
Because this consciousness arises from the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) spontaneously as a single class in constant succession,
there is no possibility for a separate view of "mine" (*mamakāradṛṣṭi*) to arise;
furthermore, within a single moment of mind, it is impossible for two distinct objects, such as permanence and so forth, to be apprehended simultaneously through separate grasping.
Furthermore, one should not say that the two types of grasping occur sequentially;
for this has functioned as a single category from beginningless time.
Thus it is said that the notion of "I" and the grasping at a self are constantly associated.
This means that because one grasps that [object] as "my self," two terms are used for the single referent of the view. In the state prior to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*),
it takes only the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) as its object.
If the basis has already been transformed and it universally takes all phenomena as its object,

because the wisdom of equality (samatājñāna) takes both the ultimate and the conventional as its objects, then "taking deliberation as its nature and characteristic" refers to the fourth intrinsic nature and the fifth aspect of activity.
Its intrinsic nature consists in deliberation following upon the mind,
as it takes that very [mind] as its mode of activity; by this,
the specific name established for it is also explained.
Because it is able to deliberate with thorough scrutiny, it is called *manas*.
In the state prior to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), it constantly and thoroughly deliberates upon the characteristics of the grasped self;

in the state after the transformation of the basis, it likewise thoroughly deliberates upon the characteristic of non-self. Regarding the phrase "the four afflictions always accompany [it]," this refers to its association with the six types of the four delusions.
In this context, "simultaneous" (*saha*) signifies the meaning of association (*samprayoga*).
That is to say, from beginningless time until the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*),
this manas spontaneously and constantly takes the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) as its object.
It is associated with the four root afflictions, namely:
self-delusion (*ātma-moha*), self-view (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), self-love (*ātma-sneha*), and self-pride (*ātma-māna*). Regarding these, "self-delusion" refers to ignorance (*avidyā*);
it is the state of being deluded regarding the characteristic of a self because one is confused about non-self (*anātman*).
The view of self refers to the grasping at a self,
because one falsely conceptualizes a self within phenomena that are not-self.
The conceit of "I am" refers to haughtiness.
Because one gives rise to arrogance by relying on the self that is grasped;
"self-love" refers to craving for the self, because one gives rise to attachment toward the grasped self.
This also indicates that pride and love are accompanied by views and pride.
This refutes the tenets of other schools who maintain that there is no such thing as association (*samprayoga*).
These four [defilements] constantly arise, agitating and turbidifying the internal mind, causing the external evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) to perpetually become defiled.
Sentient beings, because of this, transmigrate through the cycle of birth and death and are unable to attain liberation.
Therefore, they are called afflictions (*kleśa*).
There are ten kinds of them;
why are there only four here?
Because the view of self exists, other views do not arise;
for there cannot be two cognitions within a single moment of mind.
How, then, could this consciousness necessarily possess the view of self?
The two types of grasping and false views arise solely from discrimination and are abandoned only by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*);
the afflictions associated with them are exclusively innate (*sahaja*) and are therefore abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
The view of self-identity (*ātmagrāha-dṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*) arise based upon the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*).
Because this [view] is associated with [the view of self] and does not rely on that [other view],
and because one constantly clings internally to a self, there must necessarily be the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*).
Since this view is definitive and decisive, there is no room for doubt to arise.
Because of attachment to a self, hatred cannot arise;

therefore, this consciousness is associated with only four afflictions, as well as with other factors such as contact (*sparśa*) that are concomitant with the seventh [consciousness], which corresponds to these.
In this context, the word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of a collective conjunction.
As for the term "the rest," it indicates the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*);
that is to say, it shows that the manas is not only associated with the four aforementioned delusions.
Furthermore, because it also arises simultaneously with other secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), such as contact (*sparśa*) and so forth,
there are eighteen mental factors associated with this manas.
These consist of the four aforementioned afflictions [plus the others].
The five factors beginning with contact,
the eight secondary afflictions,
and the discernment (prajñā) among the object-specific mental factors.
There are four meanings of "affliction" as previously explained.
As for the mention of "contact" (*sparśa*) and so forth, it is because these five universal mental factors (*pañca-sarvatraga*) are necessarily associated [with all minds].
Furthermore, the eight secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) pervade and defile the mind.
Because the obscured-unspecified mind is a defiled mind,
although the view of self is subsumed under the wisdom of the separately fixed objects,
it is opened as a separate category because there is a difference in meaning.
For what reason does this manas lack other mental factors?
It is because the ten [factors] such as anger have coarse and agitated modes of activity, whereas this consciousness is subtle and refined; therefore, it does not coexist with them.
Although lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) are unwholesome (*akuśala*),
because these [two] are neutral (*avyākṛta*), they do not associate with them.
This refers to the desire and aspiration for an object that has not yet been attained.
This consciousness spontaneously takes as its object whatever it encounters;
whereas resolute belief (adhimokṣa) maintains and confirms objects that have never been previously determined,
this consciousness has from beginningless time always taken determined objects as its domain.
Mindfulness functions as the clear recollection of previously experienced objects.
This consciousness constantly takes as its object the phenomena currently manifested by itself.
It is invariably characterized by binding the mind to focus single-pointedly on one direction.
This consciousness functions spontaneously, perceiving objects moment by moment;
therefore, it does not coexist with the four object-specific mental factors (*viṣayapratiniyatavijñāna*).
It is exclusively wholesome and pure.
This consciousness is defiled;
therefore, it is not associated with faith and the other [wholesome factors].
*Kaukṛtya* (remorse) is the regret for actions previously committed.
This consciousness arises internally based on present objects; sleep occurs solely through the power of external conditions.
Vitarka and vicāra function by taking coarse and subtle external objects as their conditions;
since they belong to only one category,
these four indeterminate factors do not coexist with the four afflictions.
Since beginningless time, it has spontaneously and consistently taken the internal as its object, grasping at a self that is eternally without change;
because it is not associated with changing sensations,
it is therefore associated exclusively with the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*).
In the stage prior to the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti), it is not associated with the mental factors previously mentioned;
in the stage where the basis has been transformed, it arises only in conjunction with twenty-one mental factors,
just like the eighth consciousness.
In the stage where the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) has already occurred, [the mind] is associated exclusively with neutral sensation (*upekṣā-vedanā*),

because it arises spontaneously and always functions with equanimity toward its objects. Regarding the inclusion within the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) category, this is the eighth [point] concerning the analysis of the three natures.
Because these four afflictions associated with this manas are defiled,
they obstruct the Noble Path and conceal one's own mind; therefore,
they are called "obscured" (nivṛta).
It is called "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*) because it is neither wholesome nor unwholesome.
As mentioned above, because all afflictions belonging to the two higher realms are sustained by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they are indeterminate.
Furthermore, the subtle basis upon which these associated defiled phenomena rely functions spontaneously; therefore, it too is included within the indeterminate.
If the basis has already been transformed, it is exclusively of a wholesome nature; it is bound to whichever stage (bhūmi) it arises in and is connected with.
That is to say, the manas-vijñāna arises following the ālaya-vijñāna;
it is bound to the stage in which that [ālaya-vijñāna] arises.
If the mental factors associated with the manifest manas arise in the desire realm, they are bound to the desire realm;
it should be understood that this is likewise up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
This is because [the manas] spontaneously and constantly takes the ālayavijñāna as its object within its own stage, grasping it as an internal self rather than as belonging to another stage.
If the maturation ālayavijñāna of that stage manifests before one, it is called "being born in that stage.
The afflicted manas takes that as its object and grasps it as "I";
thus, being bound to that stage, it is said to be "bound by that stage."
Some say that being bound by the afflictions and so forth of a particular stage is called "being bound by that [stage]";

once the basis has been transformed (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), one is no longer bound. Regarding the Arhat’s meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and so forth, these constitute the tenth stage of abandonment and suppression.
The term "Arhat" generally indicates the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) within the three vehicles.
Because at this stage both the seeds and the active manifestations of the afflicted manas (*kliṣṭamanas*) have been eternally severed and extinguished, it is said that they do not exist.

It is said that [the afflicted mind] does not exist within the stages of training (*śaikṣa*), the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), and the supramundane path (*lokottaramārga*), because it is temporarily suppressed and ceased in all of these.
This means that the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭamanas*) has, from beginningless time, functioned as a subtle, uniform, and spontaneous process.
The various contaminated paths (*sāsrava-mārga*) cannot subdue or extinguish [the afflictions];
the noble paths of the three vehicles (*triyāna-āryamārga*), however, possess the capacity to subdue and extinguish them,
because the realization of true selflessness (*anātman*) contradicts the grasping at a self (*ātmagrāha*).
When the subsequently attained (pṛṣṭhalabdha) uncontaminated state manifests,
it is its outflow (niṣyanda) and likewise contradicts this [conventional] intention.
Because both the true realization of selflessness and the subsequently attained state are uncontaminated, they are called the supramundane path (lokottaramārga).
Since the attainment of cessation is an outflow of the noble path and is utterly tranquil,
it too does not exist [in that state]; however,
because its seeds have not been permanently severed, it is not yet absent.
Once one has emerged from the noble path following the attainment of the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*),
this [defiled mind] manifests once again until it is extinguished.
However, because these afflictions associated with the defiled mind (*kliṣṭamanas*) are innate (*sahaja*), they are not to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-prahātavya*).
Because it is defiled, it is not that which is not to be abandoned;
because it is extremely subtle, all its seeds are severed simultaneously with the lowest-of-the-low afflictions of the stage below the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
Because their power is equal,
when the diamond-like concentration (vajropama-samādhi) manifests,
one suddenly severs these seeds and becomes an Arhat.
Therefore, those in the stage of no-more-learning never again give rise [to such afflictions].
When those of the two vehicles who have attained no-more-learning turn toward the Mahāyāna,
from their initial generation of the bodhicitta until they attain Buddhahood, [they remain free from them].
Although they are in fact bodhisattvas, they are also called arhats;
because their meanings are equivalent, they are not mentioned separately.
Regarding the statement that the three stages lack the manas:
This is stated in terms of the defiled aspect;
it does not mean that the pure aspect is absent.
It is like saying that while the four stages lack the *ālayavijñāna*, it is not that the eighth consciousness is non-existent.
This should also be understood in the same way.
This mental differentiation is briefly of three kinds:
first, that associated with the view of a personal self (pudgala-ātma-dṛṣṭi).
The first is associated with the view of a self in phenomena;
the second is associated with the wisdom of equality.
The former pervades the mental states of all ordinary beings, the śaikṣas of the two vehicles, and a class of bodhisattvas prior to the seventh bhūmi who possess outflowing (sāsrava) minds.
Taking that ālayavijñāna as an object, one gives rise to the view of a person (pudgala-dṛṣṭi).

Subsequently, this occurs throughout the continuums of all ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and at all stages when the fruit of the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā-jñāna) is present for bodhisattvas.
Taking that maturation-consciousness as its object, it gives rise to the view of a self in phenomena (*dharmātman*).

Subsequently, throughout the continuum of all Tathāgatas, and during the stages of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) of Bodhisattvas, when the fruit of the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmyajñāna*) manifests before them.
Taking that stainless ripening consciousness as its object, it gives rise to the wisdom of equality;
at the stage when the view of a personal self arises,
the view of a phenomenal self also manifests.
The grasping at a self also arises based on the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*),
just as one must first be deluded by a tree stump before perceiving it as a person and so forth.
Although the functions of the two views— the view of a self and the view of phenomena— differ, [they are nonetheless related].
Yet they are not mutually contradictory,
as they both rely upon the same wisdom; it is just as,
for example, although the essence of visual consciousness and the others is one, [they function differently].
Furthermore, since there is no contradiction in the frequent occurrence of the discernment of blue and other such objects,
this case should likewise be so:
when the noble path of the śaikṣas of the two vehicles or the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) is present before them.
When Bodhisattvas of sudden enlightenment are at the stage of the path of cultivation,
and when the fruit of the wisdom realizing the emptiness of persons arises before them during their gradual realization,
they all give rise to attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).
Because self-grasping has already been subdued,

when the fruit of the wisdom realizing the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-nairātmya) does not manifest for those in the stage of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa) of the two vehicles or for this [bodhisattva] who awakens gradually,
they likewise give rise only to grasping at phenomena (dharma-grāha).
Because self-grasping has been severed,
all forms of self-grasping belonging to bodhisattvas from the eighth stage upward never manifest again;
this is because they have either been permanently severed or permanently suppressed.
When the fruit of the wisdom of dharma-emptiness has not yet manifested,
one still gives rise to attachment to dharmas;
this is because there is no contradiction [between the two].
Although the manas associated with the clinging to phenomena is said to be non-defiled for those of the two vehicles and so forth,
it is also called defiled for bodhisattvas,
because it obstructs their wisdom.
Therefore, this is also called "obscured-neutral" (nivṛta-avyākṛta); however,
for the followers of the Two Vehicles and others, it is called "unobscured" (anivṛta),
because it does not obstruct their wisdom.
This is born of maturation (*vipākaja*),
because it arises at all times from the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*);
it is not itself a fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*).
Because this name is general,
just as those not included among the other [conditions] are all subsumed under the condition of predominance (*adhipatipratyaya*),
so too has the second transformation been explained.
What are the characteristics of the third transformative consciousness?
The verse says:
Next, the third transformative consciousness Is differentiated into six kinds.
"Taking the apprehension of objects as its nature and characteristics"— this is the commentary on [the states of] wholesome, unwholesome, and neither.
From here below, nine verses reveal the third transformation.
Within this, there is a general analysis by way of eight sections:
first, to reveal the sequence;
second, to reveal the names and categories.
1. The intrinsic nature of the three types of knowledge;
2. The characteristics of their modes of activity;
3. Their classification according to the three natures.
Sixth, the analysis of mental factors;
seventh, the explanation of various feelings;
eighth, the clarification of the stages of arising.
Although there are eight sections, they are subsumed into three parts.
First, one verse clarifies the first five sections;
next, six verses clarify the various mental factors (*caitasika*).
The following two verses reveal the stages of manifestation;
this is the first verse. Next, the phrase "the third transformation" indicates the sequence.
Therefore, the treatise explains:

Next, following the transformation of consciousness as mental application (*manas*), one should distinguish the characteristics of the transformation of consciousness that cognizes objects. Regarding the statement "there are six types," this distinguishes their names and categories;
these distinctions of this consciousness comprise six types in total.
Because they differ according to the types of objects of the six sense faculties,
they are designated as "eye-consciousness" up to "mind-consciousness"; thus,
they are named according to their respective faculties.
Because it possesses five characteristics.
These five are: being the basis, that which arises, that which belongs to, that which assists, and being like a root.
Although all six groups of consciousness arise in dependence upon the mind (manas), [only the manas is designated as the "basis"].
However, it is established by way of its unique [characteristic] as "mental consciousness" (*manovijñāna*),
so that there is no risk of confusion with the five bodies of sensory consciousness.
Alternatively, it is called "mental consciousness" because it relies solely upon the mind (*manas*).
Recognition is what receives the name;
mind and mental factors are not analogous.
Thus, they are designated as "form-consciousness" up to "dharma-consciousness."
The name is established according to the object,
in accordance with the meaning of "cognition" (*vijñāna*);
that is to say, the discernment of the six objects is called "cognition."
The five consciousnesses, such as that of form and so forth, cognize only form and so forth;
the consciousness of phenomena (dharmavijñāna) is able to cognize all phenomena universally, or is able to discern phenomena.
Only the consciousness of phenomena (dharmavijñāna) receives this name;
therefore, there is no confusion regarding the names of the six consciousnesses.
Subsequently, the names of the six consciousnesses are established according to their respective objects.
This is explained based on the state where the five material sense-faculties have not yet attained mastery.
If mastery were attained, the various faculties would function interchangeably,
such that a single faculty would give rise to consciousness and perceive all objects.
However, one may simply follow the sense faculties (indriya) without the fault of confusion.
Yet, because the objects (ālambana) and supports (āśraya) of the six evolving consciousnesses are coarse, manifest, and universally established, they are not mentioned here.
To say that "cognizing objects" is their nature and characteristic (lakṣaṇa) simultaneously reveals both the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) and the mode of activity (ākāra) of the six consciousnesses.
Because consciousness has discernment as its intrinsic nature,
it takes that very [nature] as its mode of activity; by this,
the specific name established for it is also explained.
Because that which is able to discern objects is called consciousness (*vijñāna*), [the text] states "wholesome, unwholesome, and neither" to reveal the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
That which is able to bring about benefit and advantage for this life and future lives is called wholesome (*kuśala*).
Although the fruits of pleasure for humans and devas can provide benefit in this world,
they do not do so in other worlds;
therefore, they are not called "wholesome."
They are called unwholesome because they cause harm and opposition in both this world and other worlds.
Although the bitter fruits of the miserable realms cause harm in this world,
they do not do so in other worlds.
Therefore, it is not unwholesome.
Because it cannot be designated as either beneficial or harmful within the context of wholesome or unwholesome matters,
it is called "indeterminate" (avyākṛta).
"Neither" refers to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
It is called "neither" because it is neither wholesome nor unwholesome.
These six evolving consciousnesses, when associated with the eleven [mental factors] such as faith (*śraddhā*) and so forth, [are wholesome].
That which is subsumed under the category of the wholesome is associated with the ten factors such as non-greed;
that which is subsumed under the category of the unwholesome is likewise associated [with its own set]; and that which is subsumed under the category of the indeterminate is dissociated from both.
Although the three natures do not coexist within each individual consciousness,
there is the possibility of their coexistence within a collection of the six consciousnesses;
for it is possible for the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness— whether occurring as sudden or continuous, and whether few or many— to arise simultaneously.
If the three natures (trividha-svabhāva) arise simultaneously within the five consciousnesses,
the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) accords with whichever [nature] it predominantly attends;
if it does not attend to any one [in particular], it is of an indeterminate nature (avyākṛta).
Next, the sixth section explains the characteristics of mental factors (*caitta*).
The treatise should state their arising as follows:
"With how many mental factors are the six consciousnesses associated?"
The verse says: These mental factors— universal, object-specific, virtuous, afflictive,
secondary afflictive, and indeterminate— all are compatible with the three types of feeling.
The commentary states:
Among the mental factors (*caitasika*), they are broadly divided into two [sections].
First, there is one verse that generally indicates the six categories.
There are five verses following this that provide a detailed explanation of the distinctions;
this [verse] is the general heading.
The verse says "these," referring to these six evolving consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ vijñānakāya*).
The term "mental factors" (caitta) refers collectively to the six categories.
The phrase "the universal, etc. enumerates the names of these six categories.
This indicates that these six consciousnesses are universally associated with the mental factors belonging to these six categories.
That is to say, because they arise constantly in dependence upon the mind, are associated with the mind, and are bound to the mind, they are called "mental factors" (caitta).
This is just as things belonging to a self are designated by the term "belonging to the self" (ātmīya).
The mind apprehends only the general characteristics (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa) of its object;
the mental factors (caitta) also apprehend the specific characteristics (viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa) therein, assisting in the accomplishment of the mind's activity,
and thus receive the name "mental factors."
It is like a master painter creating a model and filling it with colors;
the corresponding meanings have already been explained previously.
Although the names and meanings of the various mental factors (*caitta*) are infinite, [the essential points are as follows].
There are six categories of distinctions:
namely, the five universal [mental factors] and the five object-specific ones.
There are eleven wholesome [factors],
six afflictions,
and twenty secondary afflictions.
There are four indeterminate [factors].
Thus, these six categories comprise fifty-one [mental states],
as they are invariably obtainable within all moments of consciousness.
Because they arise by taking various distinct objects as their conditions;
because they can only arise within a wholesome state of mind;
and because their nature is subsumed under the category of root afflictions.
Because these are exclusively of the nature of fundamental outflow (*niṣyanda*),
and because they are indeterminate with respect to being wholesome, defiled, and so forth,
there are thus six distinct stages. That "all are associated with the three feelings" refers to the seventh gate, the gate of association with feeling (*vedanā-saṃprayoga*).
These six evolving consciousnesses are easily detached and unstable;
they are not only associated with these mental factors,
but also arise simultaneously with the three types of feeling.
Because they all apprehend the non-dual characteristics of the agreeable, the disagreeable, and the neutral:
the apprehension of the characteristic of an agreeable object that pervasively gladdens body and mind is called pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*);
the apprehension of the characteristic of a disagreeable object that oppresses body and mind is called painful feeling (*duḥkha-vedanā*).
The perception of a neutral range of objects, which is neither oppressive nor pleasing to the body and mind, is called the sensation of neither-pain-nor-pleasure (*aduḥkhāsukhavedanā*).
These three sensations may each be divided into two:
those associated with the five sensory consciousnesses are termed bodily sensations (*kāyikī vedanā*).
Because it relies on a distinct basis,
that which is associated with the mental consciousness is called mental feeling;
because it relies solely on the mind.
Furthermore, they both encompass the two aspects of being contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*),
because painful feeling (*duḥkhavedanā*) also arises from the uncontaminated.
Alternatively, each may be divided into three.
That is to say: those abandoned by seeing, those abandoned by cultivation, and those not to be abandoned;
furthermore, there are three categories consisting of the trainee (śaikṣa), the one beyond training (aśaikṣa), and those who are neither.
Alternatively, they may be divided into four in total.
That is to say, there are the wholesome, the unwholesome, and the two types of neutral—obscured and unobscured—feelings.
Alternatively, they are divided into five in total:
suffering, pleasure, grief, joy, and equanimity.
Among the three [feelings], suffering and pleasure are each divided into two,
because the characteristics of that which afflicts and that which gratifies the body and mind differ respectively,
and because they are non-conceptual and conceptual respectively.
This is because there is a distinction between what is heavy and what is light;
as for neither-painful-nor-pleasant [feeling], it is not divided into two,
because its characteristic— being neither oppressive nor gratifying— is without difference.
Because they are non-conceptual and because they function with equality,
these three feelings may coexist with the five sensory consciousnesses.
Because objects that are agreeable, disagreeable, or neutral may all be experienced;
because the mental consciousness is not necessarily identical to the five sensory consciousnesses;
and because a single feeling arises toward an object to which attention is exclusively directed.
Because one who is without partiality gives rise only to equanimity (*upekṣā*),
the three feelings may coexist during the stage of non-mastery; however, in the stage of mastery,
there are only joy (*prīti*), bliss (*sukha*), and equanimity.
Since all Buddhas have already severed the causes of suffering and grief,
the following section extensively analyzes the mental factors (*caitta*) across six stages,
divided into five parts consisting of five verses each.
First, there is one verse that clarifies the former two characteristics.
Next, there is one verse that explains the wholesome mental factors (*citta-saṃprayukta-dharma*).
Following that, there is half a verse that explains the root afflictions (*mūla-kleśa*).
Next, there are two verses explaining the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
Following that, there is a half-verse clarifying the four indeterminate factors (*aniyata*).
Within the treatise, the first two characteristics of their arising are stated as follows:
Furthermore, what are the characteristics of the first two stages?
The verse says:
The first consists of the omnipresent factors, such as contact; the next are the object-specific factors, namely desire.
"Resolve, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom— The objects of these focal points are not the same.
Commentary:
The first phrase of the verse reveals their universal characteristics (*sarvatraga*).

Among the six categories [of mental factors], the first group consists of the five omnipresent mental factors (*sarvatraga-citta-saṃprayukta-dharma*): contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manasikāra*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*).

Since the verse mentions "contact and so forth," it refers to these five by citing the first and the remaining four. Contact is defined as having the nature of causing the mind and mental factors to encounter their objects through the differentiation of transformation resulting from the conjunction of the three [the sense organ, the object, and consciousness].
Its function is to serve as the basis for sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), volition (*cetanā*), and so forth.
That is to say, because the sense faculty, the object, and consciousness mutually accord with one another, they are called the "threefold conjunction" (*trikasamnipāta*).
Contact (*sparśa*) arises depending upon them and causes them to harmonize; therefore, it is said to have them as its basis.
The state of the threefold conjunction possesses the functional capacity to give rise to mental factors in accordance with it, and is thus termed "transformation.
Contact arises resembling that [capacity], and is therefore called "discrimination.
It causes all minds and mental factors to harmonize so as to contact their respective objects.
This contact is the intrinsic nature [of the faculty].
Since it resembles the functional capacity that gives rise to mental factors in accordance with [the object],
its function consists in serving as the basis for feeling and so forth.
If this [mental engagement] did not exist, there would be no harmonious conjunction for the purpose of contacting a single object. Mental engagement (manasikāra) has the nature of alerting the mind;
its function is to direct the mind toward the focal object.
This means that mental attention (*manasikāra*) is so called because it awakens the seeds of the mind that are to arise, drawing them toward their objects.
If this were absent, the mind would necessarily fail to cognize its objects.

Although this [mind] is also capable of inducing mental factors (*caitta*), because the mind is the primary [agent], it is said only to induce the mind. Feeling (*vedanā*) has as its nature the experiencing of objects that are favorable, unfavorable, or neutral.
Its function is to give rise to craving, because it can produce the desire for union, separation, or neither.
If this [feeling] were absent, the mind would not give rise to the mental aspects of joy, grief, or equanimity. Perception (saṃjñā) has the nature of grasping the image of an object.
Its function is the establishment of various conventional designations (*nāma-paññatti*).
That is to say, it is only by establishing the specific characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the boundaries of objects that one can subsequently give rise to various conventional designations.
If the mind lacked this [function], how could it apprehend the specific characteristics of the boundaries of objects? Volition (*cetanā*) has the nature of causing the mind to perform an action.
Its function is to employ the mind with respect to the wholesome, the unwholesome, and so forth;
that is to say, it is able to grasp the objective sphere and its primary causes and characteristics, thereby directing the mind to produce wholesome states and the like.
For if this [mental faculty] were absent, the mind would certainly be unable to produce the wholesome or the unwholesome.
From this it is proven that the five dharmas beginning with contact (sparśa) necessarily arise with the mind;
therefore, they are called "universal" (sarvatraga).
Next are the "object-specific" (viṣayapratiniyata) [mental factors].
This means that from desire up to wisdom, the objects and entities they take as focal points (*ālambana*) are for the most part different.
Because [desire] is explained first among the six stages, one might ask: what is desire?
Its nature is the aspiration for an object that is pleasing.
Its function is to rely upon diligence.
The "desired object" refers to the object that one wishes to contemplate.
When one wishes to examine any object, desire arises only because there is an expectation;
if one does not wish to examine it and instead allows the mind to engage spontaneously according to the force of its causes, no desire whatsoever will arise.
For this reason, it is said that desire is not omnipresent (*sarvatraga*).
If desire for wholesome phenomena (*kuśala-dharma-chanda*) can give rise to right effort (*samyag-vyāyāma*),
it assists in the accomplishment of all wholesome deeds.
Therefore, the treatise states that the function of this diligence is to serve as a basis. What is resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*)?
Its nature is to maintain a firm conviction regarding a determined object;
its function is to be unshakable by others.
It refers to the thorough determination and confirmation regarding an object of apprehension through the power of scripture, reasoning, and realization—whether they be erroneous or correct.
Because of this, one cannot be led astray by other conditions;
therefore, there is a complete absence of indecision regarding the object of resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*).
Since it is neither a state of deliberative resolve nor a state of resolute conviction, this resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) is also not omnipresent (*sarvatraga*). What is mindfulness (*smṛti*)?
Its nature is to cause the mind to clearly remember and not forget an object previously experienced.
Its function is to serve as the basis for meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
