because it is produced according to one's mental vows.
What need is there for it to serve as a basis for experiencing the fruits of birth and death?
For the sake of personally realizing awakening and benefiting and gladdening others,

[he teaches] because Pratyekabuddhas of indeterminate lineage, Śrāvakas, and Bodhisattvas who have attained mastery through great vows have already permanently severed or suppressed the afflictive obstructions.
There was no longer any possibility of receiving further bodies subject to the cycle of birth and death,
for fear that it would interrupt their long-term cultivation of the bodhisattva practices;
consequently, by means of the power of aspiration and untainted, supreme meditative concentration, they...
Just as the factors that sustain life serve as the cause for the present body,
causing its results to be experienced continuously over a long period,
so too do such fixed vows repeatedly provide assistance until one attains unsurpassed bodhi.
Furthermore, why would he require the assistance of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)?
Since the cognitive obstructions obstruct great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*),
he retains his body for a long duration in order to sever them.
Furthermore, the cognitive obscuration (jñeyāvaraṇa) serves as the basis for the outflows (sāsrava).
If this obscuration were absent,
those [outflows] would certainly not exist.
Therefore, it provides great assistance for the abiding of the body.

From this, one should know that the nature of the transformative birth-and-death (*pariṇāma-vaiparītya-jāti-maraṇa*) is comprised within the outflowing ripened fruit (*sāsrava-vipākaphala*), whereas with respect to uncontaminated karma (*anāsrava-karma*), it is the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
Since the cycle of birth-and-death throughout the past, future, and middle limits does not depend on external conditions but arises from internal consciousness, [it is established].
It should be understood that the continuity of pure dharmas is likewise.

That is to say, from beginningless time, untainted seeds have been attached to the fundamental consciousness; through the repeated and successive arousal by the evolving consciousnesses and so forth, they gradually increase and become more excellent.
Until finally, at the time of attaining Buddhahood,
one completely abandons the originally existing seeds of defiled consciousness and acquires the newly arisen seeds of pure consciousness.
It sustains all seeds of merit;
through the power of its original vows,
it gives rise to various sublime functions that continue uninterruptedly until the end of the future.
From this, one should know that there is only internal consciousness.
The preceding section has concluded the explanation regarding objections concerning logical inconsistency.
Below, the next six verses explain objections concerning scriptural authority.
The first three verses explain the objection concerning the contradiction with the three natures (*trisvabhāva*);
the latter three verses explain the objection concerning the contradiction with the absence of nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).
Regarding the introduction to the discussion that explains the former objection, it says:
If there is only consciousness,
for what reason did the Blessed One teach the existence of the three natures in various sūtras?
It should be understood that these three natures, too, do not exist apart from consciousness.
Why is this so? The verse says:
"By means of various conceptualizations, one conceptualizes various things."
This imagined nature does not exist at all;
the dependent nature arises from conditions;
and the perfected nature is therein perpetually devoid of the former nature.
Therefore, this [nature] and its basis for others are neither non-different nor different, just like the nature of impermanence and so forth;
it is not that one does not see this when seeing that.
Thus he explains.
These three verses explain the difficulty regarding the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
The first verse clarifies the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature).
Within it, the first phrase reveals that which performs the imagining (*parikalpa*).
The second [section] indicates the object that is the basis of pervasive conceptualization;
only in the latter half is the subject that performs pervasive conceptualization (the parikalpaka) presented.
This means that because the sixth and seventh consciousnesses engage in pervasive conceptualization, they are called "pervasive conceptualization" (*parikalpa*).
Because their categories are manifold, they are referred to as "this and that.
Conceptualizing and discriminating is what constitutes the "agent of pervasive conceptualization" (*parikalpaka*).
Because the five [sensory] consciousnesses and the eighth consciousness lack discursive investigation (*vitarka-vicāra*),
those who grasp at a self and phenomena must necessarily do so by means of wisdom (*prajñā*).
This is because the eighth consciousness is not associated with wisdom.
Although the five consciousnesses are associated with subtle wisdom,
they spontaneously take objects as their domain without conceptualization; likewise,
although the manas does not universally take all objects as its domain, [it is associated with subtle wisdom].
It is also called the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*),
because it is capable of grasping categories.
That which is the object of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*) is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Because the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) serves as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the mind and its mental factors,
the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is not their objective domain;
for the ultimate reality is not an object-condition for false conceptualization.
According to the sequential explanation, [the dependent nature] is also that which is thoroughly conceptualized (*parikalpya*).
Although the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is its object,
it is not that which is thoroughly conceptualized because it is not an objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
What are the characteristics of the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), and how does it differ from the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*)?

It is said that all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), by the power of habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*), manifest two divisions; because these arise from conditions, they are all the dependent nature.
Based on this, the pervasive imagination falsely clings to [things] as being definitely existent or non-existent, identical or different, both or neither, and so forth;
these two alone are termed the "thoroughly imagined nature" (parikalpita-svabhāva).
This imagined nature is entirely non-existent.
Because it cannot be apprehended through logical analysis according to the teachings.
The subsequent half-verse clarifies the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*):
"That which is called 'discrimination' is produced by conditions."
Since all defiled and pure minds and mental factors are termed "discrimination" because they specifically and universally engage their objects,
then all defiled and pure dependent natures (*paratantra-svabhāva*) are subsumed within this [category of] the dependent nature.
The latter one and a half verses clarify the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature).
Specifically, the first two lines directly reveal its nature;
the subsequent three lines demonstrate that it is neither identical to nor different from the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature).
The fourth phrase clarifies that by realizing this, one understands that the dependent nature is like an illusion;
the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is so named because it is the true reality of all phenomena as revealed by the two kinds of emptiness.
This reveals that the nature of this [reality] is pervasive and eternal, and is not false or erroneous.
It distinguishes itself from self-characteristics, common characteristics, space, the self (*ātman*), and so forth.
Furthermore, untainted conditioned phenomena (*anāsrava-saṃskṛta*)—which are free from inversion and possess ultimate, supreme functions that are all-pervasive—also receive this name.
However, the present verse speaks of the former and not the latter.
This refers to that which is eternally free from the aforementioned parikalpita (imagined nature) upon the paratantra (dependent nature);
its essence is the suchness (tathatā) revealed by the two kinds of emptiness.
The statement "in that" (tatra) indicates that the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) and the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) are neither identical nor separate.
The statement "always far removed" (nityam viviktam) indicates that the duality of subject and object as falsely grasped is eternally non-existent in principle.
The meaning of the preceding statement reveals that the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is not empty;
the meaning of "nature" (*svabhāva*) reveals that the two kinds of emptiness are not the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*),
because true suchness (*tathatā*) is by nature free from both existence and non-existence.
For the reasons stated above,
this perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) is neither different from nor non-different from that dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva). If it were different,
then True Suchness (tathatā) would not be the actual nature of that [dependent nature].
If it were not different from this nature, it would have to be impermanent;
both [the subject and object] would have to be pure, rather than the object being impure;
and there would be no distinction between the functions of the original and subsequent cognitions.
Just as that nature of impermanence, selflessness, and so forth is neither identical to nor different from phenomena such as the conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*),
if it were different, those phenomena would not be impermanent and so on;
if it were not different, it could not be their universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
By this analogy, it is shown that this perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) and the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) are neither identical nor different.
This must necessarily be the case according to the principle of phenomena (*dharma*) and their true nature (*dharmatā*),
because they are established in mutual dependence as the ultimate (*paramārtha*) and the conventional (*saṃvṛti*).
It is not possible to perceive that dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) without having realized and seen this perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva);
for as long as one has not attained the realization that the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) is empty,
one does not know the dependent nature as it truly is.
Once non-conceptual wisdom has realized suchness,
it is only within subsequent wisdom that one is able to thoroughly comprehend the dependent nature as being like illusory phenomena and so forth.
This is the intended meaning here.
The three natures are all inseparable from the mind and mental factors;
that is to say, because the mind, mental factors, and their manifestations arise from various conditions,
they are like magical illusions— non-existent yet appearing to exist, deceiving and deluding the foolish.
All these are termed the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Regarding this, the foolish arbitrarily grasp at the self and phenomena as being existent or non-existent, identical or different, both or neither, and so forth;
yet, like flowers in the sky, their nature and characteristics are entirely non-existent.
All [phenomena] are termed the "thoroughly imagined" (parikalpita).
Upon the "other-dependent" (paratantra), that which is falsely grasped as self and dharmas is empty;
the true nature of consciousness and so forth, revealed by this emptiness, is called the "perfectly established" (pariniṣpanna).
Therefore, these three are not separate from mind and its concomitants.
As for space, cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), under which of the three natures are they subsumed?
They may be subsumed within all three natures.
The mind and its associates transform into appearances resembling space and so forth; because they arise following the mind, they are subsumed under the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Fools falsely grasp these as being truly existent;
this is what is subsumed under the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
If the meanings such as "space" are provisionally designated upon true thusness (tathatā), they are subsumed under the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva).
Contaminated minds and so forth definitely belong to the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva).
Uncontaminated minds and so forth may be subsumed under either of the two natures.
Because it arises from various conditions, it is subsumed under the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*);
because it is free from inversion, it is subsumed under the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
How are the three natures and the five categories (*pañcavastu*) mutually subsumed?
The various sacred teachings state that the mutual inclusion of these characteristics is not fixed;
they speak according to the meaning of non-confusion regarding their characteristics.
According to this [view], the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) includes those characteristics, names, conceptualization (vikalpa), and correct cognition (samyag-jñāna).
The perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) subsumes that suchness (tathatā).
The imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) does not subsume the five categories.
It is said that the contaminated mental states and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma), which manifest as if they were the signified objects, are called "characteristics" (nimitta).
That which appears as if it were a signifier is designated as "name" (nāman).
The transforming mind and its associates are established as "conceptualization" (vikalpa).
Because untainted minds and their associates are free from conceptual proliferation (prapañca), they are not so classified.
However, these are collectively termed "correct cognition" (samyagjñāna),
without distinguishing between the signifier and the signified.
All four [of these] arise from conditions and are thus dependently originated (paratantra).
How are the spheres of activity of the three gates of liberation subsumed within these three natures? In principle, they all pertain to all three;
however, according to their specific characteristics, each corresponds to one.
One should know that emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness correspond respectively [to the imagined, dependent, and perfected natures].
Based on this, there further arise three types of the patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*):
first, the patience regarding the non-arising of intrinsic nature;
second, the patience regarding the non-arising of spontaneity.
The three types of patience regarding the non-arising of delusions and suffering correspond respectively to these [three], as they are the objects of these [patiences].
How do these three subsume those two truths?
One should know that the conventional possesses these three types,
while the ultimate is exclusively the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
There are three [types] of the conventional.
First, the conventional of designation;
second, the conventional of practice;
third, the conventional of clear manifestation.
One should understand that these three natures correspond respectively to the three types of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
The first is the ultimate reality as object (*arthaparamārtha*).
This means that suchness is the supreme object;
second, the attainment of the supreme object,
meaning that nirvāṇa is the supreme object.
The ultimate meaning of the three types of practice refers to the fact that the noble path itself is the supreme object;
it is unchanging and non-erroneous according to its respective application.
All are subsumed within the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Regarding these three natures, which are the objects of what kind of cognition?
The thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is not an object of cognition at all.
Because that which lacks intrinsic nature cannot serve as an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*),
the foolish grasp it as existent,
whereas the noble ones realize its non-existence.
It may also be described as the cognitive domain of both ordinary beings and noble ones;
the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) is the range of activity for both types of wisdom,
whereas the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) is the cognitive domain of noble wisdom alone.
Among these three natures, how many are provisional and how many are real?
Because the thoroughly imagined nature is falsely established, it may be said to be provisional.
Because it lacks any substantial essence or characteristics, it is neither provisional nor real.
The dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) is both substantially existent and nominally existent.
It is said to be nominally existent because it consists of the states of the continuity of the collection [of aggregates].
It is said to be substantially existent because the mind, mental factors, and form arise from conditions.
If substantial dharmas do not exist,
then conventional dharmas also do not exist,
because conventional dharmas are designated in dependence upon substantial causes.
The thoroughly established nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) is exclusively real existence,
because it is not designated in dependence upon other conditions.
Are these three [natures] different or non-different?
One should say that it is neither [identical nor different],
because there is no separate essence and because one falsely clings to the distinction between dependent origination and its true meaning.
The meanings and categories of these three natures (*trisvabhāva*) are boundless;
fearing that the text would become overly prolix, I have briefly indicated the essential framework.
From here on, I shall provide a general explanation to resolve difficulties regarding the three non-natures (*triniḥsvabhāvatā*).
The *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* states:
"If the three natures exist,
how is it that the Blessed One taught that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*)?"
The verse says:
Based precisely upon these three natures, the three absences of nature are established;
therefore, with intentional meaning, the Buddha taught that all phenomena are without nature.
The first is the naturelessness of characteristics; Next is the absence of a self-nature;
And finally, by being remote from the former, The nature of the grasped self and phenomena— This is the ultimate reality of all dharmas, Which is also suchness itself.
"Because it is always as its own nature, it is the true nature of consciousness-only.
The commentary states:
This explains and resolves the difficulty regarding the three kinds of non-nature (*trividhā niḥsvabhāvatā*).
The text consists of three sections.
The first verse provides a general explanation of how the three natures of non-essence (trividha-niḥsvabhāvatā) are established based on the three natures (trisvabhāva).
The subsequent verses explicitly reveal the meaning of establishing the three natures of non-essence based on the three natures.
The subsequent verse again clarifies the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Based on the three natures previously explained, those three kinds of non-nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) subsequently taught are established;
namely, the non-nature of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*), the non-nature of arising (*utpatti-niḥsvabhāvatā*), and the non-nature of the ultimate (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*).
Therefore, the Buddha spoke with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
This does not mean that their nature is entirely non-existent;
the use of the term "intentional meaning" indicates that this is not a definitive teaching (*nītārtha*).
This means that although the latter two natures are not non-existent in essence,
there are deluded beings who superimpose upon them the false attachment that they possess a real self-nature of persons and phenomena;
this is precisely what is called the "thoroughly imagined nature" (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
In order to eliminate this attachment,
the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has taught that both existence and non-existence are, in general, devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
How is it that those three [natures] are established based upon this?
That is to say, based on this first [nature], the imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva), one establishes the absence of nature in terms of characteristics (lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā);
because its essential characteristic is ultimately non-existent, like a flower in the sky.
Based on the second, the dependent (paratantra-svabhāva), one establishes the absence of nature in terms of production (utpatti-niḥsvabhāvatā).
This is like a magical illusion, produced in dependence upon various conditions.
Because it lacks the inherent nature as it is falsely grasped, it is conventionally described as being "without nature";
it is not that its nature is entirely non-existent.
Based on the subsequently attained perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), the ultimate lack of nature (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*) is established;

that is to say, the ultimate itself is conventionally described as "lacking nature" because it is devoid of the two natures of the previously mentioned imagined subject and object (*parikalpita-pudgala-dharma*).
It is not that nature is entirely non-existent.
Just as the great empty space pervades all forms yet is manifested by the absence of nature in those various forms,
so too, although the dependent nature is not the ultimate reality, it may also be described as the "naturelessness of the ultimate."
However, because it would overlap with the second [nature], it is not mentioned here.
This nature is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of all phenomena,
for it is the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) of all dharmas.
However, there are briefly four types of ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*):
first, the worldly ultimate (*loka-paramārtha*),
which refers to the aggregates (*skandha*), sense bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).
Second is the ultimate truth of reasoning,
which refers to the four truths, such as suffering and so forth.
Third is the ultimate truth of realization.
The first refers to the true suchness of the two kinds of emptiness.
The fourth refers to the ultimate of the ultimate,
which is the single true dharma-realm.
Among these, the ultimate truth (paramārtha) is explained according to the last [of the four] positions.
This last position is so called because it is the object traversed by the supreme path;
thus, this statement is made in order to distinguish it from the preceding three.
This ultimate meaning of all phenomena is also suchness (*tathatā*).
"Such" (*tatha*) means true reality, signifying that it is not false or deceptive;
"ness" (*tā*) means constant, indicating that it is without change or alteration.
This means that because this reality remains eternally as it is in its own nature across all states, it is called *tathatā* (suchness).
This signifies the sense of being serene and non-illusory.
Furthermore, the phrase "also" indicates that this [reality] has many other names.
This refers to what is called the dharma-dhātu, the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), and so forth,
as explained extensively according to their respective meanings in other treatises.
This nature is precisely the true nature of consciousness-only (vijñaptimātratā).
The nature of consciousness-only is briefly of two kinds.
The first is the false,
namely the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
The second is reality,
which refers to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
The term "real nature" is used to distinguish it from that which is false and illusory.
Furthermore, there are two natures:
the first is the conventional,
which refers to the dependent nature.
The second is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*),
which refers to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
It is called "real nature" (*tattva*) in order to distinguish it from the conventional.
These three verses collectively demonstrate that the statements regarding the absence of nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) found throughout the various sūtras are not of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Therefore, those who possess wisdom should not rely upon them to categorically deny that all phenomena possess any intrinsic nature whatsoever.
Having extensively analyzed the nature and characteristics of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*),
the following third section consists of five verses that explain the stages of practice within that consciousness-only.
The text introducing these five stages states:
Regarding this nature and characteristic of consciousness-only thus established:
who enters it, at how many stages, and in what manner?
It is said that those who possess the two types of Mahāyāna lineage [enter].
Briefly stated, one enters [the path] gradually through five stages.
What are the two kinds of lineage (*gotra*) in the Mahāyāna?
First, the naturally abiding lineage (*prakṛtistha-gotra*).

This refers to: first, the cause of untainted dharmas obtained by the very nature of things (*dharmatā-pratilabdha*), which has been attached to the fundamental consciousness since beginningless time;
and second, the lineage (*gotra*) accomplished through cultivation, which arises after one has heard the dharmas that flow forth from the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-niṣyanda*).

The [nature] formed by the perfuming of that which is accomplished through hearing and so forth requires the possession of these two types of Mahāyāna lineage in order to be able to gradually awaken to and enter into vijñaptimātratā.
What are the five stages of entering into consciousness-only?
First is the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*),
which refers to the cultivation of the Mahāyāna factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣa-bhāgīya*).
2. The stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*), which refers to cultivating the Mahāyāna aids to penetration (*nirvedha-bhāgīya*).
3. The stage of thorough comprehension (*prativedha-avasthā*).
This refers to the path of seeing (darśanamārga) in which bodhisattvas abide,
and the four stages of cultivation (bhāvanāvasthā),
which refer to the path of meditation (bhāvanāmārga) in which bodhisattvas abide.
Fifth is the stage of culmination,
which refers to abiding in unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
How does one gradually awaken to and enter into representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*)?
This means that bodhisattvas, during the stage of the equipment for the nature and characteristics of consciousness, are able to develop profound faith and understanding;
and during the stage of application, they are able to gradually suppress and eliminate the grasped and the grasper, thereby inducing true vision.
In the stage of penetration (*prativedha-avasthā*), one penetrates reality as it truly is;
in the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*), one repeatedly cultivates the principle realized therein to suppress and sever remaining obstacles;
and upon reaching the ultimate stage (*niṣṭhā-avasthā*), one emerges from obstacles into perfect clarity.
Being able to transform sentient beings throughout the entirety of the future and further causing them to awaken to and enter into the characteristics and nature of consciousness-only—
what are the characteristics of the initial stage of the equipment (sambhāra-avasthā)?
The verse says:
"Until consciousness has arisen, one seeks to abide in the nature of representation-only;
yet regarding the latent tendencies of the two graspings, one has not yet been able to subdue or extinguish them.
Commentary: This reveals the first stage, the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*).
From the initial generation of the profound and firm mind of great bodhicitta,

until one has not yet given rise to the consciousness that accords with the stage of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) and seeks to abide in the true ultimate nature of representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*),
all such stages are subsumed within the level of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*).
Within this, the stages of the ten abodes, the ten practices, and the ten dedications are subsumed,
as one cultivates and accumulates various supreme provisions for the sake of attaining unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
For the sake of sentient beings, they diligently seek liberation;
for this reason, it is also called the "factor conducive to liberation" (*mokṣabhāgīya*).
In this stage, the bodhisattva relies upon four superior powers: the power of the cause, the power of a spiritual friend, the power of mental attention, and the power of the provisions.
Although they have deep faith and understanding in the meaning of Vijñapti-mātra, they have not yet realized the emptiness of the grasped and the grasper.
Because they dwell mostly in the external gate while practicing the bodhisattva path,
they still lack the power to suppress and eliminate the latent tendencies (anuśaya) induced by the two graspings, such that those two graspings do not arise as manifest activity.
The term "these two graspings" (dvaya-grāha) indicates the grasping of the two graspings,
because it refers to the grasping of the nature of the grasper and the grasped.
The accumulation of the habituation of these two graspings is called their latent tendencies (anuśaya).
They are called "proclivities" (anuśaya) because they follow after sentient beings, lie dormant within the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), or increase their faults; that is to say,
they are the seeds of the afflictive obstructions (kleśāvaraṇa) among the objects of knowledge.
The afflictive hindrance refers to the one hundred and twenty-eight root afflictions, headed by the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*),
which clings to a real self as being conceptually constructed.
Together with their outflows and various secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*),
these all disturb and afflict the body and mind of sentient beings and are able to obstruct *nirvāṇa*;
thus they are called the afflictive obstruction (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
The cognitive obscuration refers to those factors headed by the view of a personal identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), which clings to the imagined nature of phenomena as being real,
including [the views of] wrong views, doubt, ignorance, craving, hatred, pride, and so forth.
The nature of non-erroneousness regarding the objects of knowledge that are obscured, which can obstruct bodhi,
is called the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
This cognitive obscuration is definitely not concomitant with the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).
Because it is weak and inferior;
because it is not associated with the wisdom that is free from ignorance;
and because it arises simultaneously with the fruit of the knowledge of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-jñāna*).
Among the seven transformative consciousnesses,
they are either few or many according to their respective applications, as explained in the case of the afflictions.
This is because the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, are devoid of conceptual discrimination (*avikalpaka*).
The various views, doubt, and so forth are definitely not associated with it;
the others may all be induced by the power of the mind.
This hindrance is associated only with the two types of mind: the unwholesome and the indeterminate.
The treatises state that the signless (*animitta*) applies exclusively to the unwholesome (*akuśala*) and neutral (*avyākṛta*) natures;
furthermore, because delusion (*moha*) and non-delusion (*amoha*) are not associated,
this hindrance must necessarily exist within the hindrance of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Because that concentration takes this as its basis,
although their essential natures are not different, their functions are distinct; thus,
due to the superiority or inferiority of the functions of the two types of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) in relation to the Noble Path, there is a sequence in the abandonment of the afflictions.
Among the unobscured-neutral states, this is of the nature of maturation-born (*vipākaja*),
and not the other three types; for those,
such as the postures (*airyāpathika*), have weak functional power.
It is not "unobscured" because it obscures the realization of bodhi through the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*);
it is called "unobscured" only in relation to the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
If viewed from the perspective of a bodhisattva,
it is also obscured;
this refers to the cognitive obstructions (jñeyāvaraṇa) that possess views, doubt, and so forth.
How is it that this kind of sūtra describes it as the "ground of the abiding of ignorance" (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*)?
Because ignorance is predominant, it is collectively termed "ignorance," though this does not mean that views and other afflictions are absent.
Just as the seeds of afflictions are established under the names of the four abodes of attachment— namely, attachment to the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the realm of existence,
along with views and ignorance— is it not the case that pride, ignorance,
and so forth do not exist there? Likewise, those [afflictions] among the two obstructions that arise through discrimination are subsumed under what is abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*).
Those that arise spontaneously are subsumed under what is abandoned through cultivation.
The followers of the two vehicles can only abandon the afflictive hindrances,
whereas Bodhisattvas abandon both.
The permanent severance of these two types occurs only through the Noble Path;
however, the suppression of their active manifestation can be achieved through both the impure path and the Noble Path.
A bodhisattva abiding in this stage of the equipment (sambhāra-avasthā) [is capable of this].
Although there may be suppression of the coarse active manifestations,
regarding the subtle ones and the two types of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), the power of calm abiding and insight (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) is still weak and unable to suppress or eliminate them.
At this stage, one has not yet realized the suchness (*tathatā*) of consciousness-only.
One should know that practicing various superior practices by the power of resolute belief is also subsumed within the stage of practice through belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*).
What are the characteristics of these practiced superior activities?
Briefly, there are two kinds:
namely, merit and wisdom.
Among all superior practices, those whose nature is discernment are termed wisdom.
The remainder is called merit (*puṇya*).
Furthermore, based on the general characteristics of the six *pāramitās*, all are twofold;
however, according to their specific characteristics, the first five are said to be merit.
The sixth is wisdom; alternatively, the first three are comprised solely of merit, while the last one is solely wisdom.
The remaining ones pertain to both types.
Furthermore, there are two kinds:
namely, benefiting oneself and benefiting others.
All the superior practices cultivated through the power of one's aspirational resolve pertain universally to both the practice of benefiting oneself and benefiting others.
Speaking according to their specific characteristics,
the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), and so forth are subsumed under practices for one’s own benefit;
the four means of attraction (*catvāri saṃgrahavastūni*), the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*), and so forth are all subsumed under practices for the benefit of others.
Such distinctions among these practices are boundless,
and all are the sublime practices cultivated within this stage.
Although the two obstacles have not yet been suppressed or eliminated at this level, there are three types of regression that may occur while cultivating these sublime practices.
Yet, one is able to refine the mind through three matters and remains courageous and non-retrogressive in what is realized and cultivated.
First, upon hearing that unexcelled, perfect enlightenment is vast, profound, and far-reaching, the mind immediately becomes discouraged and retreats.
First, having cited those who have already realized great enlightenment, one refines one's own mind to be courageous and non-retrogressive.
Second, upon hearing that the perfections such as generosity are extremely difficult to practice, the mind may become discouraged and retreat.
First, when reflecting on one's own inclinations, one is able to cultivate the "revolving" [meditation] and other practices to train the mind with such vigor that one does not retreat.
Third, upon hearing that the Buddhas' perfect transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) is extremely difficult to realize, the mind may become discouraged and retreat.
By citing the coarse virtues of others as a contrast to one's own sublime causes, one refines one’s own mind with courageous non-retrogression.
Through these three matters, one refines the mind and,
with firm and blazing resolve, practices all supreme deeds.
Next, regarding the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*),
the Master of the Treatise raises the question:
"What are the characteristics of the subsequent stage of application?"
The verse says:
To manifest before oneself a slight object, claiming it to be the nature of consciousness-only—
because there is something apprehended— it is not truly abiding in consciousness-only.
The commentary states:
This reveals the second stage of application (*prayoga*).
First, during the first incalculable eon (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), the bodhisattva...
Having fully prepared the provisions of merit and wisdom,
and having perfected the factors conducive to liberation,
one enters the path of seeing and abides in the nature of consciousness-only.
Furthermore, one cultivates the preparatory applications (*prayoga*) to subdue and eliminate the two types of grasping;
these are the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*), Peak (*mūrdhan*), Patience (*kṣānti*), and the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
These four are collectively termed the "Aids to Penetration" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).

Because it proceeds toward the stage of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) that accords with reality and is proximate to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), it is designated by the name "application" (*prayoga*);
it is not the case that the preceding stage of equipment (*sambhāra*) lacks the sense of application.

The four dharmas, beginning with "Heat" (uṣmagata), are established based on the four thorough investigations (paryeṣaṇā) and the four kinds of knowledge of reality as it is (yathābhūtaparijñāna) in their initial and subsequent stages.
As for the four thorough investigations:
they are the investigation that names, objects, intrinsic nature, and distinctions exist only as designations (prajñapti) and lack substantial reality.
To thoroughly and accurately know these four as being devoid of consciousness and as neither existing nor non-existing is called "knowledge according to reality.
Because the name and the object differ in character, one seeks them separately;
because the two pairs share similar characteristics, one contemplates them together.

Based on the attainment of the "clarity-obtained" concentration (*ālokalabdha-samādhi*), one initiates the lower-level investigation (*vitarka*) and contemplates the non-existence of the grasped object (*grāhya*); this is established as the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*).

This means that within this stage, one first contemplates that the four factors—the name (*nāman*) and so forth—which constitute the grasped object, are all transformations of one's own mind; they are merely provisionally designated and, in reality, cannot be found.
Because they are the preliminary signs (*pūrvanimitta*) for first attaining the "Beneficial Sun," the five sciences (*pañcavidyā*) receive their name.
Since all paths thus attained are likewise preliminary signs, they are called "Heat" (*uṣmagata*).

Based on the concentration of Increasing Clarity (*vidyāvṛddhi-samādhi*), one gives rise to superior investigation (*vitarka*) and contemplates the non-existence of the apprehended object (*anupalabdha-grāhya*); this is established as the stage of "Summits" (*mūrdhan*).

This means that in this stage, one repeatedly contemplates that the four dharmas—the apprehended object and so forth—are all transformations of one's own mind, existing only as provisional designations, and that no substantial reality can be found.
Because the aspect of light becomes further transformed, it is called "increasing light" (*āloka-vṛddhi*).
Because it represents the culmination of the stage of investigation, it is further named "Summit" (mūrdhan).
Relying on the meditative concentration of conformity and compliance, one gives rise to such wisdom directed toward the lower [realms];
regarding the object of apprehension, one maintains the absence of fixed determination.
Within the absence of a grasper, there is likewise compliance with the patience of joy;
since there is no real object apart from the grasping consciousness,
how could there be a real consciousness apart from the grasped object?
Because there are five aspects of the mutual dependence between the grasped object and the grasping subject,
the stage of "patience" (kṣānti) is collectively termed "patience.
It is designated as "patience-conforming" (anulomikī-kṣānti) because it confirms what preceded and conforms to what follows.
Because the objects of cognition and consciousness are empty, it is called "patience" (*kṣānti*).

Based on the uninterrupted concentration (*ānantarya-samādhi*), one gives rise to the superior wisdom that realizes reality as it is; by sealing the emptiness of the two graspings, the "Supreme Worldly Dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*) is established.
That is to say, while the preceding "superior patience" (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) only seals the emptiness of the grasper (*grāhaka*), [the Supreme Worldly Dharma] seals the emptiness of both.
In this world, the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgradharma) is the simultaneous sealing of both emptinesses.
Because one necessarily enters the Path of Seeing immediately thereafter, it is designated by the name "uninterrupted" (ānantarya).
Among all mundane dharmas, this is the most supreme; therefore, it is called the Supreme Mundane Dharma.
In this way, during the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*) and Peak (*mūrdhan*), one contemplates the emptiness of the apprehended object based on the apprehending consciousness.
When the stage of Lower Patience (*kṣānti*) arises, one seals the characteristic of the emptiness of the object.
During the stage of Middle Patience, one accords with and accepts that the apprehending consciousness is empty, just as the object is empty.
At the stage of the arising of the highest patience (*adhimātrā kṣānti*), one seals the emptiness of the apprehending subject;
at the stage of the supreme mundane dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*), one seals both aspects of emptiness.
Because these all still involve conceptual signs (*nimitta*), they have not yet realized the truth.
Therefore, it is said that within these four stages, the bodhisattva still establishes a slight object before them,
namely, the true ultimate nature of representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
This is because the two aspects of emptiness and existence have not yet been eliminated.
Because one who contemplates with signs perceives something attained,
they do not truly abide in the nature of true consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*).
Only after those signs have ceased does one truly abide [in it].
Based on this meaning, there is a verse that says: "When a Bodhisattva is in the state of meditative equipoise, He observes that the reflected image is nothing but mind.
Once the conceptualization of objects has been eliminated,"
Examining that there is only one's own ideation,
one thus abides in the internal mind and knows that the apprehended object does not exist.
Next, the grasper is also non-existent;

subsequently, contact is found to be unapprehendable. At this stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*), the bondage of signs (*nimitta-bandhana*) has not yet been dispelled, nor has the bondage of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya-bandhana*) been severed.
It can only suppress and eliminate the two types of conceptual grasping because they contradict the Path of Seeing; however,
regarding the innate [grasping] and the two latent tendencies, the mind of impure contemplation still apprehends them as having objective existence.
Because conceptual discrimination still exists,
[these afflictions] have not been entirely subdued and eliminated,
nor have they been completely extinguished.
In this stage, the bodhisattva practices the observation of both the established truths (*vyavasthāpita-satya*) and the non-established truth (*avyavasthāpita-satya*),
in order to induce the two types of path of vision (*darśana-mārga*) in the future and to suppress the two types of conceptual obstacles (*vikalpa-āvaraṇa*).
The non-established truths (*apratiṣṭhita-satya*) are what is correctly contemplated;
it is not as with the two vehicles, who contemplate only the established [truths].
It is by giving rise to these roots of goodness, such as "heat" (*uṣmagata*), that the bodhisattva proceeds.
Although the stage of preparation may involve all the dhyānas,
it is only by relying on the fourth that it reaches fulfillment,
because one enters the path of seeing by depending upon the most excellent basis.
Only based on a body within the fortunate realms of the desire realm does one give rise to other forms of wisdom and the mind of renunciation,
for these are not yet superior;
this stage is also subsumed under the Stage of Practice through Understanding (adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi).
Because the true ultimate reality of Vijñapti-mātra has not yet been realized,
what are the characteristics of the subsequent stage of penetration?
The verse says:
When, with respect to the object of cognition, wisdom finds nothing at all,
at that time one abides in consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), because one is free from the characteristics of the two graspings.
Commentary:
This reveals the third stage, the stage of thorough penetration (*prativedha*).
At that time, the Bodhisattva, regarding the objects of focus, attains non-apprehension through non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*),
because they do not grasp at the various signs of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
At that time, one is said to truly abide in the ultimate nature of consciousness-only;
that is, the wisdom that realizes suchness is equal to suchness itself,
for both are free from the characteristics of the grasper and the grasped.
Both the characteristics of the grasped object and the grasping subject are conceptual constructions,
because they manifest as the proliferation of discursive thought based on the attainment of something existing. Therefore,
while there is no objective part (nimittabhāga), there is a subjective part (darśanabhāga).
It is said that there is no grasping because it does not grasp at signs;
although it possesses the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*), it does not engage in discrimination and is therefore said not to be a grasper (*grāhaka*).
It is not that apprehension is entirely non-existent;
although there is no objective aspect (nimittabhāga), it can be said that this [apprehension] arises bearing the semblance of suchness,
because it is not separate from suchness.
Just as the self-cognizing part (svasaṃvitti-bhāga) cognizes the seeing part (darśana-bhāga) without undergoing transformation while cognizing it,
this [case] should likewise be so.
If it were to cognize through transformation, it would not be a direct realization.
Because subsequent attainment wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) involves conceptualization,
when this wisdom arises immediately after the preparatory stage (*prayoga*),
its realization of suchness (*tathatā*) is termed the stage of penetration (*prativedha-avasthā*).
Because it first illuminates the principle, it is also called the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Briefly stated, this Path of Seeing is of two kinds:
first, the True Path of Seeing (*tattvadarśanamārga*).
This refers to the aforementioned non-conceptual wisdom,
which truly realizes the ultimate truth revealed by the two kinds of emptiness and truly eradicates the latent tendencies of the two obstacles of conceptualization.
The two emptinesses and the two obscurations are realized and severed simultaneously;
because of the power of their resolute intention (*āśaya*), they possess the capacity [for this],
even though the matter is only fully completed over many moments.
Because their characteristics are identical, they are collectively termed "one mind.
Second is the path of insight (*darśanamārga*),
which further consists of two types.
In the first contemplation of the non-established truths, there are three grades of mind.
First, the wisdom that internally eliminates the objects of the conventional designation of sentient beings and phenomena;
it is capable of removing the weak-grade latent tendencies of conceptualization.
Second, the wisdom that internally dispels the conventional designations of all phenomena as objects can eliminate the middling-grade latent tendencies of conceptualization.
Third, the wisdom that universally dispels the conventional designations of all phenomena pertaining to all sentient beings as objects.
It is able to eliminate all latent tendencies of conceptual discrimination.
The first two are called "dharma-knowledge" (dharmajñāna) because they each take their respective objects individually.
The third is the subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*).
Because it takes [the truths] collectively as its object,

it consists of the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) regarding the two types of emptiness within the true path of dharma (*dharmābhisamaya*), which sever the respective obstacles to be abandoned.
The path of insight (*darśanamārga*) is established through both specific and general designations.
Regarding the two [types], there are sixteen moments of mind that take the conventionally established truths (*prajñaptisatya*) as their object.
These, in turn, are of two kinds.
First, based on the observation of the distinction between the grasped object (*grāhya*) and the grasping subject (*grāhaka*), sixteen types of mind are established as categories.
Specifically, regarding the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), there are four types of mind:
first, the patience of the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*).
This refers to contemplating the suchness (*tathatā*) of the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) within the three realms,
thereby correctly abandoning the twenty-eight types of conceptual proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering in the three realms;
it constitutes the two types of dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhadharmajñāna*).
That is to say: the patience that immediately follows [the preceding] contemplates the previously [realized] suchness;
it realizes liberation from the afflictions manifested by that [suchness];
and it is the subsequent dharma-knowledge patience regarding the three types of suffering.
This refers to the arising of untainted wisdom immediately following [mundane] knowledge,
wherein the patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) regarding phenomena are each individually realized within.
It is said that all subsequent noble dharmas (*āryadharma*) are of this same category.
The subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna).
This refers to the arising of uncontaminated knowledge immediately following that [subsequent cognition of suffering],
which definitively confirms and validates the subsequent cognition of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti).
Just as there are four types of minds regarding the truth of suffering,
it should be understood that the same applies to the truths of origin, cessation, and the path.
These constitute the sixteen moments of mind.
The eight [aspects] are the contemplation of suchness and the contemplation of correct wisdom.

Within the path of seeing the reality of phenomena (*dharmatā-darśanamārga*), there are the uninterrupted (*ānantarya*) and liberation (*vimukti*) paths, as well as the self-verified aspects (*svasaṃvedana-bhāga*).
These are established as the distinctions of the path of seeing based on names and characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa-darśanamārga*).
Second, based on the contemplation of the objects of the truths regarding the higher and lower realms, sixteen distinct types of mental states are established.
That is to say, for each of the four truths—suffering and so forth—within both the manifest and non-manifest realms, there are two mental states.
First, the patience of clear realization (*abhisamayakṣānti*);
second, the wisdom of clear realization (*abhisamayajñāna*).

These are, as appropriate, the uninterrupted path and the path of liberation within the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), consisting of the vision-aspect (*darśanabhāga*) that perceives the truths.
The one hundred and twelve types of conceptual proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of cessation are called the Path of Vision of Characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-darśanamārga*).
All Paths of Vision of Characteristics are conventionally designated as such based on the [ultimate] truth.
It is not actually the case that the Supreme Mundane Dharmas arise immediately and sever the latent dispositions (anuśaya),
because they can only arise after the true Path of Seeing (darśanamārga).
Because one does not establish [the conventional] after having already established the non-established;
because the latent tendencies of conceptualization have been truly severed;
and because the preceding true path of vision realizes the nature of consciousness-only.
The subsequent path of seeing realizes the characteristic of consciousness-only;
it is subsumed under the fundamental wisdom of the preceding true path of seeing,
while the subsequent path of seeing is subsumed under the subsequently attained wisdom.
Because the first of these two is superior, it is specifically mentioned in the verse.
When a bodhisattva attains these two paths of vision (*darśanamārga*),
they are born into the abode of the Tathāgata and dwell in the Stage of Extreme Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
Having thoroughly mastered the dharma-realm, they attain all forms of equality.
They are constantly born within the great assemblies of all Buddhas and have attained mastery over many hundreds of gateways.

Knowing for oneself that one will soon realize great enlightenment and be able to bring benefit and happiness to all beings throughout the future, one next enters the stage of cultivation. What are its characteristics?
The verse says:
"Non-apprehension and inconceivability are supramundane wisdom;
because they abandon the two types of coarse heaviness (dauṣṭhulya), one realizes the transformation of the basis (āśrayaparāvṛtti).
Commentary:
This reveals the fourth stage, the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
Having emerged from the preceding path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*),
the bodhisattva acts to sever the remaining obstacles and realize the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
Furthermore, one repeatedly cultivates non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
Because this wisdom is free from the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*),
it is said to be without attainment and inconceivable (*acintya*).
Alternatively, it is described as "non-attainment" because it is free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*);
it is called "inconceivable" because its wondrous function is difficult to fathom;
it is the supramundane non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
Because it severs the mundane, it is called "supramundane.
The latent tendencies of the two types of grasping are the root of the mundane;
only this [wisdom] can sever them and thus alone earns the name.
Alternatively, the designation "supramundane" is established based on two meanings:
namely, its essence being untainted (*anāsrava*) and its realization of *tathatā*.
Because this wisdom possesses these two types of meaning, it alone is termed supramundane.
Other forms of wisdom are not like this;
because non-conceptual wisdom within the ten stages is cultivated repeatedly, one abandons the two types of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*).
The seeds of the two obstacles are designated by the term "coarse heaviness."
Because its nature lacks functional capacity and contradicts subtlety and lightness,
it causes those [defilements] to be eternally extinguished; therefore, it is called "equanimity" (*upekṣā*),
as it is able to abandon those two types of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*).
One is then able to realize two kinds of transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
"Basis" refers to that which serves as a support;
specifically, it refers to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), because it serves as the support for both defiled and purified phenomena.
"Defilement" refers to the false and pervasive parikalpita (imagined nature);
"purity" refers to the true pariniṣpanna (perfected nature);
and "transformation" refers to the relinquishing of the former and the attaining of the latter within these two aspects.
By repeatedly cultivating non-conceptual wisdom, one eliminates the coarse latencies (*dausthulya*) of the two obscurations within the fundamental consciousness;
thus, one is able to transform and abandon the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) that exists upon the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Furthermore, one is able to transform and attain the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*);
by transforming the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*), one attains great nirvāṇa,
and by transforming the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), one realizes unsurpassed enlightenment.
The purpose of establishing the doctrine of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) is for sentient beings to realize the fruit of these two types of transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
Alternatively, the "basis" refers to the suchness (*tathatā*) of consciousness-only.
Because it is the basis for both birth-and-death and nirvāṇa,
foolish people, through their inverted views, are deluded regarding this true suchness;
thus, from time immemorial, they have undergone the suffering of birth-and-death.
The Noble One, having realized this True Suchness (tathatā) free from inversion,
attains nirvāṇa and ultimate peace and bliss;
for by repeatedly cultivating non-conceptual wisdom, they sever the heavy residues (dauṣṭhulya) of the two obstacles within the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna).
It is able to transform and attain a basis like that of saṃsāra,
and it is able to transform and attain a basis like that of nirvāṇa;
this is precisely suchness (tathatā) as the nature free from defilement.
Just as it is inherently pure yet inherently defiled by nature,
when it is freed from defilement, it is conventionally described as newly purified;
this very new purification is termed the "transformation of the basis" (āśraya-parāvṛtti).
In the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*), one abandons the obstructions and realizes [enlightenment];
although bodhi is indeed attained at this stage,
it is not what is intended to be expressed by the meaning of this verse.
The meaning of the verse is simply to reveal the transformation of the nature of consciousness-only.
That which is called the "body of liberation" (vimuktikāya) at the stage of fulfillment for the two vehicles is called the "dharma-body" (dharmakāya) in reference to the Great Sage.
How are the two kinds of transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) realized?
It is by cultivating the ten superior practices within the ten stages (bhūmi),
severing the ten heavy obstacles, and realizing the ten aspects of suchness (tathatā).
By this, the two kinds of transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) are realized.
Regarding the ten stages (bhūmi):
the first is the Stage of Supreme Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi).
First is the Stage of Attaining the Holy Nature (*Prathamābhūmi*), so called because one first attains the holy nature and fully realizes the two kinds of emptiness,
thereby benefiting oneself and others and giving rise to great joy.
Second is the Stainless Stage (*Vimalābhūmi*).
Possessing pure ethical discipline (*śīla*),
because one has distanced oneself from the defilements of afflictions that give rise to even subtle transgressions;
this is the third stage, the Radiant Stage (*prabhākari-bhūmi*).
The Fourth Ground, the Radiant (Arciṣmatī), because one achieves the great dharma-dhāraṇī of supreme meditative concentration and is able to emit the boundless light of wondrous wisdom.
Abiding securely in the supreme factors of enlightenment,
because the flames of wisdom increase as they burn the fuel of afflictions—
this is the fifth stage, the Extremely Difficult to Conquer (Sudurjayā).

The sixth stage, the Stage of Manifestation (*Abhimukhī*), is so named because it is extremely difficult to overcome as it brings into correspondence the mutually contradictory activities of the two types of wisdom:
the ultimate and the conventional.

The seventh is the Far-Reaching Stage (*dūraṅgamā bhūmi*), because it brings to manifestation the supreme non-conceptual *prajñā* by means of abiding in the wisdom of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-jñāna*),
reaching the very limit of effortful engagement in the signless dwelling (*animitta-vihāra*).
Because it transcends the worldly path and the paths of the two vehicles,
it is the eighth stage, the Immovable (*acalā-bhūmi*),
wherein non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) continues spontaneously in its characteristics and functions.
Because afflictions cannot disturb it,
it is the ninth stage, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence (Sādhumatī),
wherein one accomplishes the four subtle and sublime analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid).
Because they are able to skillfully preach the Dharma throughout the ten directions.
Tenth is the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā bhūmi*):
the great cloud of Dharma-wisdom contains the waters of manifold virtues.
Because it is obscured by the coarseness (dausthulya) that is like space and because the dharmakāya is filled with [these],
these ten stages collectively subsume all conditioned and unconditioned merits as their intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
It is called a "ground" (bhūmi) because it serves as a superior support for the practices being cultivated,
enabling them to grow and flourish. The ten superior practices are the ten pāramitās.
There are three kinds of giving:
namely, the gift of material wealth, the gift of fearlessness, and the gift of the Dharma.
There are three kinds of ethical discipline.
These are the morality of restraint, the morality of gathering virtuous dharmas, and the morality of benefiting sentient beings.
There are three types of patience:
patience in enduring enmity and harm, patience in accepting suffering, and patience in the discernment of dharmas.
There are three kinds of diligence:
namely, the diligence of donning the armor, the diligence of gathering virtue, and the diligence of benefiting and bringing happiness.
There are three kinds of meditative concentration.
These are the meditative concentrations of abiding in tranquility, the meditative concentrations that induce [supernormal powers], and the meditative concentrations that accomplish tasks.
There are three kinds of prajñā:
non-conceptual wisdom regarding the emptiness of sentient beings, non-conceptual wisdom regarding the emptiness of phenomena, and non-conceptual wisdom regarding the emptiness of both.
Skillful means (upāyakauśalya) is of two kinds:
namely, skillful means of dedication (pariṇāmanā-upāyakauśalya) and skillful means of deliverance (uddharaṇa-upāyakauśalya).
Aspiration (praṇidhāna) is of two kinds.
This refers to the aspiration for enlightenment and the aspiration to bring benefit and happiness to others.
There are two kinds of power:
the power of analytical reflection (*cintā-vicaya-bala*) and the power of cultivation (*bhāvanā-bala*).
Wisdom is of two kinds:
namely, the wisdom that experiences the joy of the Dharma and the wisdom that brings sentient beings to maturity.
As for the nature of these ten:
Generosity has as its nature non-attachment and the three types of action arising therefrom;
ethical discipline has as its nature the three types of action at the time of undertaking and training in the bodhisattva precepts;
and patience has as its nature non-aversion, diligence, discerning wisdom, and the three types of action arising therefrom.
Vigor has as its nature diligence and the three types of action (karma) arising therefrom;
meditative concentration has as its nature only samādhi;
and the final five all have as their nature the discernment of phenomena (dharmapravicaya).
Because these are said to be the fundamental and subsequently attained wisdoms (*mūla-prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*),
among them, the eighth has desire, resolve, and faith as its nature,
because it takes these three as its own essence (*svabhāva*).
This explains their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Together with their retinues, each and every one has all co-arising virtues as its nature.
These are the ten aspects.
The pāramitās can only be established when they are embraced by seven types of supremacy.
First is the supremacy of abiding,
which means that one must abide within the bodhisattva lineage.
Second is the excellence of the basis,
which means that one must rely upon the great bodhicitta.
Third is the excellence of the intention.
That is to say, one must have compassion for all sentient beings;
this is the most excellent of the four activities.
That is to say, one must fully carry out all activities; this is the most excellent of the four activities.
Fifth is the supremacy of skillful means,
which must be embraced by signless wisdom (*animitta-jñāna*).
Sixth is the supremacy of dedication (*pariṇāmana*).
That is to say, it must be dedicated toward unsurpassed enlightenment;
this is the supreme excellence of the seven purities.
That is to say, it must not be interspersed with the two obstacles.
If these practices of giving and so forth are not embraced by these seven [perfections], they do not constitute "pāramitās" (arriving at the other shore). Therefore,
each of the ten pāramitās, including giving and the rest, should be analyzed according to the fourfold logical alternatives (catuṣkoṭi).
Regarding why there are exactly ten and neither more nor less:
it is because within the ten stages (bhūmi), one realizes ten suchnesses (tathatā) by counteracting ten obstacles, and thus there is neither increase nor decrease.
As for the first six of these, they are neither more nor less [for the same reason].
That is to say, the three beginning with generosity are the path to higher rebirth,
because they bring about great wealth, a physical body, and a retinue;
the three beginning with diligence are the path to definitive excellence.
Because they can subdue afflictions, ripen sentient beings, and [fulfill] the Buddha-dharmas,
the path of all bodhisattvas consists of only these two.
As for the latter four, they serve as aids to the former six, ensuring that their cultivation is brought to fulfillment without increase or decrease.
Skillful means assists the three [perfections] beginning with generosity;
aspiration assists diligence;
and power assists meditative concentration.
Wisdom assists prajñā by causing it to be cultivated to fulfillment.
As for the ten stages in sequence,
this means that each preceding stage induces and brings forth each succeeding one.
Furthermore, because each subsequent stage maintains the purity of each preceding one,
and because each preceding stage is coarse while each subsequent stage is subtle,
the sequence of their cultivation— whether easy or difficult— is as follows.
Regarding these ten cultivations, there are five types of cultivation:
first, cultivation based on the support of the physical basis;
second, cultivation based on mental attention (*manasikāra*).
Third, cultivation based on the resolute intention;
fourth, cultivation based on skillful means;
fifth, cultivation based on mastery.
By practicing these five modes of cultivation, one brings all ten perfections (*pāramitā*) to full completion.
As for their mutual inclusion,
each one encompasses all the perfections because they are mutually concordant.
Regarding the principle that the preceding induces the succeeding through the practice of preliminary stages:
the preceding encompasses the succeeding because the latter necessarily depends upon the former;
whereas the succeeding does not encompass the preceding because the former does not depend upon the latter.
Regarding the statement that "by practicing the subsequent [vows], one maintains the purity of the preceding":
this is because the subsequent [vows] encompass the preceding and thereby maintain the purity of the preceding;
whereas the preceding do not encompass the subsequent, and thus do not constitute maintaining its purity.
If one practices according to that which can intermingle,
one should formulate four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) by comparing them to one another.
Although these actually number ten, six are mentioned here.
It should be understood that the latter four are subsumed within the sixth;
as for their expansion into ten,
the sixth subsumes only non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
The latter four are all subsumed under subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*),
because they take conventional reality as their object.
As for these ten fruits:
There are four types of contaminated [dharmas],
excluding the fruit of dissociation.
There are four types of uncontaminated [dharmas].
Excluding the ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*),
there are instances where it is said that [a cause] possesses all five fruits;
this is either because the five characteristics mutually support one another or because two [categories] are combined in the explanation.
Regarding these ten trainings:
those subsumed by their intrinsic nature, the precepts subsume only the ethical discipline,
while meditative concentration subsumes dhyāna.
Wisdom subsumes the latter five;
if their attendants are included, they all possess mutual subsumption.
Alternatively, according to their functions, ethical discipline subsumes the first three.
Because they constitute the substance, the self-nature, and the retinue of the provisions (*sambhāra*),
meditative concentration (*samādhi*) subsumes the dhyānas,
and wisdom (*prajñā*) subsumes the latter five perfections.
Vigor comprises three [aggregates],
because it universally stimulates the three.
As for their specific manifestations, the aggregate of ethical discipline subsumes the first four.
The first three are as previously described and because they involve protection;
concentration comprises the dhyānas,
while wisdom comprises the latter five.
These ten stages of the causal state have three designations.
The first is called *pāramitā*,
referring to the first incalculable aeon (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
At that time, the power of generosity and the other perfections is still weak;
being overwhelmed by the afflictions, they have not yet been able to subdue them.
Consequently, these afflictions manifest without one's awareness.
The second is called the "near pāramitās," referring to the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa;
at that time, the power of generosity and the other perfections increases slightly.
It is not that the afflictions are subdued and then able to subdue them;
rather, it is by means of the intentional mind that the afflictions proceed.
These three are called the Great Pāramitās.
This refers to the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa.
At that time, the power of generosity and the other perfections increases further,
enabling one to ultimately subdue all afflictions.
Consequently, these afflictions never manifest again.
Although all ten are actually cultivated throughout the ten stages,
they are cultivated one by one on each stage according to their predominant characteristics.
Although the practices of the ten stages have immeasurable gateways,
they are all subsumed within the ten pāramitās.
As for the ten heavy obstacles:
First is the obstruction of the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*).
This refers to that which arises from conceptual construction (*vikalpaja*) among the two obstructions;

because the nature of an ordinary being is established based upon its seeds, when the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) of the two vehicles manifests, one is said to have attained the nature of an noble one (*āryatva*) by severing only this single type.
When the Bodhisattva’s path of seeing manifests before them, they possess the complete abandonment of these two types [of obstacles] and is said to have attained the nature of an Arya.
When the two true paths of seeing manifest before them,
those two types of hindrances are necessarily no longer established.
Just as light and darkness certainly do not arise together,
like the simultaneous rising and falling of the two ends of a balance scale,
such must necessarily be the principle for all mutually contradictory phenomena.
Therefore, there is no fault of both natures being established simultaneously.
Nevertheless, the abandonment of the two obstacles must necessarily be achieved by means of two paths;
the first is called the path of uninterrupted continuity (*ānantarya-mārga*).
The second refers to liberation.
This is because the mental orientations differ regarding the severance of afflictions and the realization of cessation;
furthermore, it is for the sake of abandoning that nature of coarse heaviness (dauṣṭhulya).
Although the seeds of the afflictions are absent during the path of uninterrupted realization (*ānantarya-mārga*),
one has not yet abandoned that state of unfitness (*akarmanyatā*);
in order to abandon this, the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) arises.
And when this is realized, it is termed the unconditioned state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Although that which is abandoned at the first stage actually pertains to both obstacles,
the obstacle of the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*) is intended here as referring to the cognitive obstacle (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*).
This is because it is taught that the ten types of ignorance are non-afflicted.
In reality, even during the stage of the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) in the first bhūmi, one also abandons a portion of the innate cognitive obscurations (jñeyāvaraṇa).
However, for the time being, only those abandoned at the very beginning are mentioned.
The abandonment [of obstacles] in the subsequent nine stages should be understood by analogy with this.
Since the time spent in the stage of full completion is already protracted,
it stands to reason that one should proceed to abandon the obstacles that ought to be abandoned.
Otherwise, there would be no distinction between the paths of the three times;
therefore, it is said that after a bodhisattva has attained clear realization (abhisamaya),
they further practice within the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) across the ten stages (daśabhūmi).
They cultivate exclusively the path that eternally extinguishes the cognitive obscurations,
yet they retain their afflictive obscurations to assist their vows for rebirth;
thus, they do not hasten toward parinirvāṇa like those of the two vehicles.
Therefore, one does not abandon the afflictions during the stage of the path of cultivation,
as they are abandoned all at once only when one is about to become a Buddha.
Second is the obstacle of wrong conduct.
This refers to a portion of the innate cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and the three types of karma resulting from transgressions committed through error;
these obstruct the extremely pure ethical discipline (*śīla*) of the second stage (*bhūmi*).
Upon entering the second stage, one is able to sever them forever.
Third is the obstacle of dullness (*mṛdu*).
This refers to a portion of the innate cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that causes one to forget what has been heard, reflected upon, and cultivated.
It obstructs the sublime meditative concentrations and dhāraṇīs of the third stage, as well as the three types of superior wisdom arising therefrom.
Upon entering the third stage, one is able to permanently sever the subtle afflictions that manifest as obstacles;

these consist of a portion of the innate aspect of the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), which is comprised of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth associated with the sixth consciousness.
Because it is of the lowest grade;
because it lacks the condition of deliberate attention (*amanasikāra*);
and because it follows along with the manifest activity (*samudācāra*) from afar.

It is called "subtle" because it previously often arose as being of the same substance as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and other such [afflictions], and thus was designated by the name "affliction.
It obstructs the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) of the fourth stage.
Upon entering the fourth stage (*bhūmi*), one is able to permanently sever [the obstacles].
Fifth is the obstacle to parinirvāṇa in the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).

This refers to a portion of the innate cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) which causes one to loathe saṃsāra and seek nirvāṇa, similar to the two lower vehicles that loathe suffering and aspire toward cessation.
That obstacle impedes the path of non-differentiation of the fifth stage;
upon entering the fifth stage, one is able to permanently sever it—
the obstacle of the manifestation of the six coarse signs.
This refers to a portion of the innate cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that consists of the active manifestation of coarse signs grasping at defilement and purity.
These obstruct the path free from defilement and purity in the sixth stage;
upon entering the sixth stage, they can be permanently severed.
The seventh is the obstacle consisting in the manifestation of subtle characteristics.
This refers to that portion of the innate cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) which involves the manifestation of subtle characteristics grasping at arising and ceasing;
it obstructs the sublime path of signlessness (*animitta-mārga*) of the seventh stage.
Upon entering the seventh stage (*bhūmi*), one is able to permanently sever the obstacles to the application of effort (*prayoga*) within the eightfold signlessness (*animitta*).
These refer to a portion of the innate cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that prevent the contemplation of signlessness from arising spontaneously.
In the first five stages, there is much contemplation with signs (*sanimitta*) and little contemplation without signs (*animitta*);
in the sixth stage, there is little contemplation with signs and much contemplation without signs;
in the seventh stage, there is exclusively contemplation without signs.
Although it is constantly continuous, there is still applied effort (*prayoga*);
