because there is applied effort within the signless (*animitta*),
one is not yet able to spontaneously manifest signs and lands.
This obstacle pertains to the effortless path (*anābhoga-mārga*) of the eighth stage;
upon entering the eighth stage, one is able to sever it forever.
Ninth is the obstacle of being unwilling to engage in the benefit of others.

This refers to a portion of the innate cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) which causes one to lack the desire to diligently engage in activities for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings, and instead delights in cultivating one's own self-interest.
These obstruct the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) of the ninth stage.
Upon entering the ninth stage, one is able to sever it forever.
Tenth is the obstacle consisting of not having attained mastery over all phenomena;
that is, a portion of the innate cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) which prevents one from attaining mastery over all phenomena.
Those obstacles to the great cloud of dharma-knowledge of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and the activities arising from what it contains can be permanently severed upon entering the tenth stage;
although one attains mastery over phenomena (*dharma*) at this stage, [the obstacles remain].
Yet there remain other obstacles that have not yet been termed "ultimate," namely:
innate subtle cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and the seeds of spontaneously arising afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

When the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests, they all simultaneously sever [these obstacles] and enter the stage of the Tathāgata; therefore, there are eleven obstacles throughout the Buddha-stage.
As for the ten suchnesses (*tathatā*):
The universal pervasion of suchness means that this suchness is revealed by the two kinds of emptiness;
because there is not a single dharma that it does not pervade.
Second is the most excellent *tathatā*.
This means that this *tathatā* possesses boundless virtues and is therefore the most supreme among all phenomena (*dharmas*).
Third is the True Suchness of the Supreme Flow;
this refers to the teaching that flows from this True Suchness,
which is far superior to all other teachings.
Fourth is the *tathatā* without appropriation;
that is to say, this *tathatā* has no point of attachment,
because it is not that upon which the grasping of self-clinging and so forth depends.
The five categories have no distinction in their suchness;
that is to say, this suchness has no differentiation among its categories,
unlike the eye and other faculties, whose categories possess distinct differences.
Sixth is the *tathatā* (suchness) that is neither defiled nor purified;
this means that this *tathatā* is by its very nature undefiled,
and it cannot be said that it becomes pure only later.
Seventh is the suchness that is without differentiation,
meaning that although this suchness is established in manifold ways through various teachings, it remains without distinction.
Eighth is the suchness that neither increases nor decreases.
This means that this suchness is free from the grasping at increase or decrease,
because it does not undergo increase or decrease according to defilement or purity.
This very suchness is also called the "suchness that is the basis for mastery over marks and lands."
This refers to the true suchness that serves as the basis for mastery over the nine knowledges,
because once this true suchness has been realized, one possesses mastery over both the manifestation of signs and the manifestation of buddha-fields.
This refers to the suchness that serves as the basis for mastery over the ten types of karmic action, because once this suchness has been realized,
one attains mastery over the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
This means that once one has realized this suchness,
one attains mastery over all supernormal powers, activities, dhāraṇīs, and meditative concentrations; thus,
although the nature of suchness is in reality without differentiation, [one exercises sovereignty over these diverse functions].
Nevertheless, ten types are provisionally established according to their predominant virtues;
although all [realities] have already been reached within the first stage (*bhūmi*),
the practice of realization is not yet perfected.
In order to bring to completion each successive stage of establishment,
the bodhisattva thus practices ten types of sublime conduct with heroic vigor throughout the ten stages (*bhūmi*). By doing so,
they sever the ten heavy obstacles and realize the ten aspects of true suchness (*tathatā*).
One is able to realize the two types of transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
Regarding the distinct stages of this transformation of the basis, there are briefly six kinds.
The first is the transformation through the weakening of power and the enhancement of capacity.
This refers to the first two stages;
by means of cultivating resolute conviction (*adhimukti*) and a sense of shame and dread of blame (*hrī-apatrāpya*),
one diminishes the power of the defiled seeds within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
It augments the functional capacity of the pure seeds within the fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
Although one has not yet severed the seeds of the obstructions and realized the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) in reality,
the gradual suppression of their active manifestation is also termed "transformation."
Second is the transformation through penetration,
which occurs during the stage of penetration;
by the power of the path of seeing, one penetrates suchness.

Third is the transformation through cultivation, which consists of severing the coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*) of the two obstacles born of conceptual discrimination and realizing a partial true transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).
This refers to the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*).
By repeatedly practicing the conduct of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*),
one eliminates the coarse latencies (*dauṣṭhulya*) of the two innate obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) through the power of shame (*hrī*).
One gradually realizes the true transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
The fourth is the transformation of the perfection of the fruits,
which refers to the stage of ultimate consummation (*niṣṭhā-bhūmi*).
Through practicing boundless and difficult supreme deeds over three great incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*),
when the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests,
one forever severs all innate coarse burdens (*dauṣṭhulya*).
Sudden realization of the Buddha-fruit and the perfection of the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti),
which brings inexhaustible benefit and happiness throughout the limits of the future;
this is the fifth, the inferior transformation.
This refers to the stage of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas),
who exclusively seek their own benefit, loathe suffering, and aspire toward quiescence;
they are able to penetrate only the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
To sever the seeds of afflictions, realize *tathatā*, and attain analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*),
yet to lack superior capability is termed "inferior transformation.
Sixth is "vast transformation."
This refers to the stage of the Mahāyāna:
for the sake of benefiting others, one proceeds toward great enlightenment,
feeling neither longing for nor aversion toward either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa.
Possessing the capacity to thoroughly penetrate the true suchness of the two kinds of emptiness,
they simultaneously sever the seeds of the cognitive and afflictive obstructions and suddenly realize unsurpassed bodhi and nirvāṇa.
That which possesses superior capability is called "vast transformation. Here,
the intended meaning is the vast transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*),
because one abandons the two types of coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) and realizes [the state] through its attainment.
The meaning of the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) briefly comprises four distinct types. First is the path that effects the transformation;
this, in turn, has two aspects.
The first is the path of suppression, which refers to suppressing the power of the latent tendencies (anuśaya) of the two obstacles.
This ensures that the two obstacles do not manifest.
It encompasses both the contaminated and uncontaminated paths, as well as the three types of wisdom— preparatory, fundamental,
and subsequent— through which these obstacles are gradually or suddenly suppressed as appropriate.
Second is the path capable of abandonment,
which refers to that which can eternally sever the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the two obstacles;
this path is certainly not an impure preparatory stage (*prayoga*).
Because they possess the characteristic of being drawn forth by a previously cultivated continuity of outflows that has not yet been extinguished;
and because they are drawn forth by the preparatory effort seeking what is to be realized, which remains unaccomplished.

Therefore, these are the latent tendencies (anuśaya) that delude regarding the principles [of reality], which are to be abandoned through vision (*darśana-heya*) and through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Because fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) directly realizes the principle (*tattva*), it is uniquely capable of correctly severing those [afflictions];
as for the remaining latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) associated with objects that are abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) and which involve delusion regarding phenomena,
both fundamental and subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) are capable of correctly severing them.
Second, the basis of transformation (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
This, in turn, has two aspects:
first, the basis that sustains the seeds (*bīja-dhāra-āśraya*).
This refers to the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna). By means of this, it is able to maintain the seeds of both defiled and pure phenomena,
and it serves as the common basis for both defiled and pure phenomena.
The Noble Path functions to cause the relinquishing of defilement and the attainment of purity.
Although other bases that arise from the various stages (*bhūmi*) are also supports, they cannot sustain the seeds; therefore, they are not mentioned here.
Second is the basis of delusion and enlightenment,
which refers to True Suchness (tathatā).
It is by virtue of this that it can serve as the fundamental ground for both delusion and enlightenment.
All defiled and pure phenomena arise in dependence upon it;
the noble path transforms them so that one abandons the defiled and attains the pure.
Although other factors may mutually serve as the basis for the phenomena of delusion and awakening, [it is this alone that is the primary support].
However, because it is not fundamental, it is not mentioned here.
Third, that which is relinquished through transformation;
this, moreover, is twofold.
First is abandonment through severance;
this refers to the seeds of the two hindrances when the true path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) is present before one.
Because the obstacles and their remedies are mutually exclusive, the former are then severed and extinguished, never to be established again;
this is called "abandonment.
Since those seeds have been severed, the false attachment to a self and phenomena no longer manifests.
The self and phenomena as they are grasped do not confront deluded cognition;
they are also said to be "abandoned.
For this reason, it is called the abandonment of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Second is that which is abandoned,
namely the remaining seeds of the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) and the inferior untainted (*anāsrava*).
These are relinquished when the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) arise.
It induces the ultimate, perfectly luminous [wisdom] that can purify the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
Since that [fundamental consciousness] is not its support, one desires to abandon it entirely.
Once those seeds have been abandoned, [the transformation is complete].
Present contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) and inferior uncontaminated phenomena (*hīna-anāsrava-dharma*) never arise again.
Since they will never arise, they are also said to be "abandoned" (*prahīṇa*).
For this reason, it is called the abandonment of the inferior phenomena of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Fourth, that which is obtained through transformation.
This, in turn, is twofold:
first, that which is obtained through manifestation.
This refers to the Great Nirvana.
Although its intrinsic nature is primordially pure,
it is rendered unmanifest by adventitious obscurations.
Because the arising of the true noble path eliminates those obstacles,
it causes their characteristics to become manifest;
this is called attaining nirvāṇa.
This is established based on True Suchness (tathatā) as being free from obstructions;
therefore, its essence is the pure Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu).
There are briefly four distinct meanings of nirvāṇa.
First is the nirvana of natural purity,
which refers to the principle of suchness regarding the characteristics of all phenomena;
although it possesses adventitious defilements, its fundamental nature is pure.
It is endowed with immeasurable and subtle merits;
being without birth or cessation, it is as capable as space.
It is equally shared by all sentient beings.
It is neither identical to nor different from all phenomena;
it is free from all marks and all conceptual discrimination;
the paths of thought are cut off and the names of speech are severed.
It is realized within by the true noble ones alone;
because its nature is fundamentally quiescent, it is called nirvāṇa.
Second is nirvāṇa with remainder.
This means that when suchness emerges from the afflictive obscurations,
although there remains a subtle suffering because its basis has not yet been extinguished,
it is called nirvāṇa because the obscurations have been eternally stilled.
Third is nirvana without remainder.
This refers to the very suchness (tathatā) emerging from the suffering of birth and death;
once the afflictions have been exhausted, the remaining basis (upadhi) is also extinguished.
It is called nirvāṇa because all suffering is eternally stilled.
Fourth is non-abiding nirvāṇa,
which refers to suchness itself emerging from the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Constantly assisted by great compassion and prajñā,
one thereby abides neither in saṃsāra nor in nirvāṇa;
this is the function that brings benefit and happiness to sentient beings until the end of the future.
Because it is eternally quiescent, it is called nirvāṇa.
All sentient beings possess the first [type];
those of the two vehicles who have attained no-more-learning may possess up to three.
Only our Blessed One possesses the four types of parinirvāṇa.
How, O Sugata, can you have a remainder of the support (sopadhiśeṣa)?
Although there is no actual support, it appears as such.
Alternatively, it is said that there is "no remainder" (anupadhiśeṣa) based on the exhaustion of suffering,
whereas it is said that there is "remainder" (sopadhiśeṣa) when the basis of suffering still exists;
therefore, the Blessed One may be said to possess all four [nirvāṇas].
Although the two vehicles lack both body and wisdom in the state of nirvana without remainder,
it is not said that they possess them because of their realization;
in that state, there is only pure suchness.
Being free from marks, they are steadfastly quiescent and at peace;
based on this, it is said that they are no different from Buddhas.
However, they lack the activity of awakening and benefiting others.
Therefore, it is further stated that this [obscuration] differs from that of a Buddha.
Since the cognitive obscuration (jñeyāvaraṇa) also obstructs nirvāṇa,
why is it said only to be an obstruction to bodhi?
One should understand that the holy teachings speak according to predominant functions;
in reality, however, both [the afflictions and the aggregates] are capable of obstructing both fruits.
Among the four types of nirvāṇa thus described:
Only the latter three types are termed "attained through manifestation.
The two [types] attained through production refer to Great Enlightenment (mahābodhi).
Although this possesses the seeds capable of producing [the result] from the very beginning,
it does not arise because it is obstructed by the objects of knowledge; however,
through the power of the Noble Path, those obstructions are suppressed.
It causes [the seeds] to arise from their seeds so that awakening is attained;
once arisen, it continues in succession until the end of the future.
This is precisely the mental complex associated with the four wisdoms.
The mental complex associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom refers to this mind which is free from all conceptual discrimination;
its objects of perception and its modes of activity are subtle and difficult to know.
It is neither deluded nor ignorant regarding any objective phenomena;
its nature and characteristics are pure, free from all defilements,
and it serves as the support for both the manifest and the seeds of purely virtuous qualities.
It is able to manifest and produce reflections of bodies, lands, and wisdom,
without interruption or transition, throughout the limits of the future,
just as a great round mirror manifests all manner of forms and images.
Second is the mental state associated with the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*).
This refers to the mental state that contemplates all phenomena and all sentient beings— both oneself and others— as entirely equal,
and which is constantly conjoined with great compassion and other such qualities.
It manifests the various distinctions of the images of the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and its lands according to the inclinations of sentient beings;
it is the unique support for the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) and is established upon non-abiding nirvāṇa (*apratiṣṭhitanirvāṇa*).
It is of a single flavor, continuous until the end of the future.
Third is the mental state associated with the wisdom of wondrous observation;
that is, this mental state proceeds without obstruction as it skillfully observes the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena.
They encompass and contemplate the gateways of immeasurable dhāraṇī-samādhis and the precious jewels of merit they generate;
within great assemblies, they are able to manifest immeasurable varieties of functional activities, attaining mastery over them all.
It rains the great rain of the Dharma,
severing all doubts and causing all sentient beings to obtain benefit and happiness.
Fourth is the mental state associated with the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).
This means that this mental state, for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings,
manifests various transformations through the three karmas throughout the ten directions,
thereby accomplishing the deeds that should be performed by the power of its original vows.

Although each of these four classes of consciousness associated with wisdom (jñāna) invariably possesses twenty-two dharmas— comprising both the transforming subject and the transformed object, as well as their seeds and manifest forms—
they are designated by the name "wisdom" because the function of wisdom is predominant.
Therefore, these four categories collectively encompass all conditioned merits of the Buddha-ground without exception.
This refers to the transformation of the mental states associated with the eight, seven, six, and five consciousnesses that were previously impure (*sāsrava*).
They are attained in this respective order.
Although wisdom is not consciousness, it evolves in dependence upon consciousness;
because consciousness is the primary factor, it is said that one attains [wisdom] by transforming consciousness.
Furthermore, in the state with outflows (*sāsrava*), wisdom is weak and consciousness is strong;
in the state without outflows (*anāsrava*), wisdom is strong and consciousness is weak.
This is for the purpose of exhorting sentient beings to rely on wisdom and abandon consciousness.
It is taught that by transforming the eight consciousnesses, these four wisdoms are attained.
Because the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom first becomes manifest at the moment of initial Buddhahood during the Path of Liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), it arises for the first time then.
However, the seeds of the maturation consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*) have not yet been suddenly abandoned when the Diamond-like Samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*) is present.
Because it is not in contradiction with the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*),
this category [of seeds] continues uninterruptedly from the initial attainment of Buddhahood until the end of the future,
as it maintains the untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) so that they are not lost.
The Bodhisattva’s Wisdom of Equality arises for the first time precisely because it contradicts the two types of grasping during the Path of Seeing; however,
because grasping has not yet been severed throughout the subsequent ten stages (*bhūmi*),
it may be interrupted at times during states such as those involving outflows (*sāsrava*).
After the Dharma-cloud stage (dharmameghā-bhūmi), it continues in succession with the purified eighth consciousness until the end of the future;

the wisdom of wondrous observation (pratyavekṣaṇājñāna) arises as part of the category of the contemplation of emptiness, and it may also first arise during the stage of insight of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha).
From this point onward, it proceeds successively up to the higher stages.
It may manifest at any time when one is not in a state of contaminated birth, during the category of the contemplation of emptiness, or when there is no mind.
The Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna) first arises upon the attainment of Buddhahood.
This is because, within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), the eyes and other sense organs transformed by the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) are not untainted (*anāsrava*).
It is impossible for tainted, non-common, necessarily concomitant, and co-objective faculties to produce an untainted consciousness.
Because it is logically inconsistent;
because these two differ in their clarity or obscurity regarding the object;
therefore, this category must necessarily attain Buddhahood.
It can only arise based on the untainted faculties (anāsrava-indriya),
yet it is frequently interrupted because it arises through mental attention (manasikāra).
Although these four natures are all inherently present from the beginning,

The fruit of Buddhahood is perfectly complete, neither increasing nor decreasing, throughout the limits of the future;
it arises solely from seeds and does not perfume them into seeds,

The first three categories of wisdom encompass all objects, both the ultimate and the conventional, and are subsumed under two types of wisdom:
because they take suchness as their object, they are categorized as non-conceptual wisdom; because they take other objects as their basis, they are categorized as subsequently attained wisdom.
Its essence is one,
yet it is divided into two according to its functions.
Because conventional reality is understood through the realization of ultimate truth, it is called "subsequently attained."
The fourth wisdom-category (jñāna-varga) universally takes as its objects all phenomena such as form across the three periods of time;
this does not contradict correct reasoning.

Because it arises in accordance with mental attention (manasikāra), takes the characteristics of things as its objects, and gives rise to transformative activity (nirmāṇa-karman), it is subsumed under subsequently attained wisdom (pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna).
These four categories of wisdom are called "attained through production.
This attainment through production is collectively termed *bodhi*.
And the previously mentioned "nirvāṇa" refers to that which is attained through transformation;
although there are four types of the meaning of transformation-basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*),
one should here take only two as the attainments resulting from transformation.
Because the verse speaks of "attaining the transformation of the basis" (āśrayaparāvṛtti),
this refers to the stage of cultivation (bhāvanā-avasthā) as being capable of attaining it,
not as having already attained it.
Because it is comprised within the causal stage,
what are the characteristics of the subsequent ultimate stage?
The verse says:
This is the untainted realm, the inconceivable, virtuous, eternal, and blissful body of liberation;
it is called the Dharma by the Great Muni.
Thus it is explained.
This reveals the fifth stage, the ultimate stage (*niṣṭhā-bhūmi*).
It should be understood that the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) attained during the preceding stage of cultivation is precisely the characteristic of this ultimate stage.
This refers to the aforementioned two fruits of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*),
which are comprised within the ultimate untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*).
In this state, all outflows (*āsrava*) are eternally exhausted, and no outflows increase therein.
Because its nature is pure, perfect, and luminous, it is called "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*).
"Realm" (*dhātu*) carries the meaning of "storehouse";
for within this, there are contained boundless and rare great merits.
Alternatively, it is in the sense of being a cause,
for it is able to produce the mundane and supramundane benefits and happiness of the five vehicles.

Although there is the manifestation of a body subject to birth and death, as well as karma, afflictions, and so forth— which resemble the truths of suffering and its origin— [it is nonetheless the truth of cessation].
In reality, they are untainted (anāsrava) and are subsumed under the Truth of the Path (mārgasatya);
as for the statement that fifteen elements (dhātu) are exclusively tainted, [it refers to the other elements].
That was stated in reference to the coarse and superficial objects of the two vehicles,
not with respect to all things; that is to say,
among the remaining eighteen elements (*dhātus*) that are fully established.
Only the latter three are subsumed under the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Although those accomplished by the Buddha are entirely untainted,
they are not the objective domain known by the followers of the two vehicles.
This fruit of the transformation of the basis is also inconceivable,
because it transcends the path of discursive thought and linguistic expression,
and because it is subtle, profound, and personally realized within.
Because it cannot be illustrated by any worldly analogies;
because it is the nature of the virtuous and pure dharmas;
and because the pure dharma-realm is utterly secure, being far removed from arising and ceasing.
Because the four wisdom-minds possess wondrous functions that are boundless and extremely skillful;
and because both types are of a nature that is concordant and beneficial.
Thus, the Noble Ones teach that cessation and the path are exclusively of a wholesome nature.
All phenomena such as the bodies and lands of all Tathāgatas are subsumed under cessation and the path,
for they are neither suffering nor its origin.
This includes the impure, unwholesome, and indeterminate appearances transformed by the consciousness of the Buddha.
All are produced from untainted wholesome seeds and are subsumed under the untainted wholesome;
furthermore, these are eternal and have no limit of exhaustion.
The pure dharma-realm is without arising and without cessation;
because its nature is immutable, it is said to be permanent.
Furthermore, because the four wisdoms and their mental factors serve as its support, they are also permanent.
Because it is without cessation or exhaustion,
it is also said to be permanent;
yet it is not permanent by way of its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Because they arise from causes,
that which arises returns to cessation;
this is because it is categorically affirmed.
It is not that form and mind are not impermanent; rather,
because there is no end to the time for those to be converted,
they continue without interruption or exhaustion until the limits of the future.
Furthermore, because it is peaceful and free from affliction,
the pure dharma-realm is tranquil in all its aspects; therefore,
it is called "peaceful bliss" (*sukha*).
The mental states associated with the four wisdoms are eternally free from afflictions;
therefore, they are called "blissful.
Both of these have a nature that is entirely devoid of oppression or distress.
Furthermore, because it can bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings,
both types of transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) are termed "peaceful bliss.
This refers to the fruits of the two types of transformation of the basis attained by those of the Two Vehicles.
Because there is no dharma superior to this that is eternally free from the bonds of the afflictive hindrances,
it is merely called the *vimuktikāya*.
The Greatly Awakened World-Honored One has accomplished the unsurpassed dharma of silence.
Therefore, he is named the Great Muni.
The two fruits attained by this Honored Muni,
which are eternally free from the two hindrances, are also called the Dharmakāya.
Because it is adorned with great meritorious qualities such as the immeasurable and boundless powers and fearlessnesses,
and because the term "body" (kāya) is used in the sense of a collection of entities and their substrates,
this Dharma-body has five dharmas as its nature.
It is not that the pure dharma-realm alone is called the dharma-body;
for both results of the two-fold transformation of the basis are subsumed within it.
Thus, the dharma-body has three distinct characteristics.
First is the svabhāvakāya (self-nature body),
which refers to the true and pure dharmadhātu (dharma-realm) of all Tathāgatas,
serving as the equal basis for the saṃbhogakāya (enjoyment body) and nirmāṇakāya (emanation body).
It is free from marks, quiescent, and transcends all conceptual proliferation;
it is endowed with boundless, true, and eternal merits,
and is the equal, ultimate nature of all phenomena.
This very intrinsic nature is also called the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*),
because it is the basis for the dharmas of great merit.
Second is the Enjoyment-body (*saṃbhogakāya*).
This is of two kinds.
First is self-enjoyment,
which refers to the boundless, true merits produced by the Tathāgatas through their cultivation and accumulation of immeasurable provisions of merit and wisdom over three incalculable eons.
And the perfectly quiescent, eternally pervasive form-body,
which continuously remains serene until the end of the future, constantly enjoys for itself the vast dharma-joy;
second, the enjoyment for others.
This means that the Tathāgatas, by means of their wisdom of equality,
manifest a subtle and pure body of merit and dwell in a land capable of purification for the sake of bodhisattvas who abide on the ten stages.
Manifesting great supernormal powers and turning the wheel of the true Dharma,
they resolve the nets of doubt for all beings, causing them to enjoy the bliss of the Mahāyāna Dharma;
these two aspects combined are called the *saṃbhogakāya* (Enjoyment Body).
Third is the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
This refers to how all Tathāgatas, by means of the wisdom of accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*),
manifest immeasurable transformation bodies that accord with the various classes of beings, dwelling in both pure and impure lands.
For the sake of the bodhisattvas who have not yet ascended the stages, as well as those of the two vehicles and ordinary beings,
he manifests supernormal powers and preaches the Dharma according to their respective capacities,
causing each to obtain various benefits and happiness.
Regarding the inclusion of the three bodies within the five natures of phenomena:
among these, the first includes the svābhāvikakāya;
it is taught that the svābhāvikakāya is eternal by nature.
This is because that which is attained through the realization of the cause is not a productive cause;
it pervades all phenomena like space,
being signless, unconditioned, and neither form nor mind.
Within the mental complex of the four wisdoms,
the eternal and omnipresent form body arising from the mirror-like wisdom (ādarśajñāna) subsumes the self-enjoyment [body],
while the Buddha-body manifested by the category of the wisdom of equality (samatājñāna) subsumes the other-enjoyment [body].
The various bodily forms manifested by the wisdom of accomplishing activities (*krtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) according to the capacities of beings are subsumed under the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*).
Since the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) subsumes the Buddha’s unique, conditioned, and real virtues, [the former is likewise included].
The four wisdoms, as well as the actual form and mind, are all subsumed under the category of enjoyment (*saṃbhoga*).
Furthermore, since both the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and the Transformation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*) are manifestations shown as skillful means for the sake of transforming others,
it cannot be said that actual wisdom constitutes their essence.
However, although the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the body of enjoyment for others (*parasaṃbhogakāya*) lack actual mind and mental factors (*citta-caittasika*),
they do possess manifested mind and mental factors;
for the supernatural power of the Unsurpassed Enlightened One is inconceivable.
He is able to manifest formless phenomena.
If it were not so, how could the Tathāgata manifest greed, anger, and the like?
Since it has been severed for a long time,
how could śrāvakas, animals, and the like know the mind of the Tathāgata?
For even bodhisattvas who have attained equal enlightenment do not truly know the mind of the Tathāgata.
According to this sutra,
it is said that [the Buddha] transforms immeasurable classes of beings, causing them all to possess minds and manifesting the three types of karmic action.
Although these three bodies all possess boundless merits,
each has its own distinct characteristics.
That is to say, the svabhāvakāya possesses only reality, permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
It is free from all defilements, the basis of all virtues,
unconditioned merit,
and devoid of the distinct characteristics and functions of form, mind, and so forth.
The body of self-enjoyment possesses immeasurable varieties of true merits, such as sublime form, mind, and so forth.

As for the body of other-enjoyment and the transformation body, they possess only the meritorious characteristics of manifesting boundless forms, minds, and so forth that resemble [the former] to benefit and bring happiness to others. Furthermore, the essential body (svābhāvikakāya) is correctly subsumed under self-benefit.
Because it is tranquil, blissful, and without activity,
it also benefits others by acting as a predominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) that enables all sentient beings to obtain benefit and happiness.
Furthermore, because it serves as the basis for both the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*),
it is comprised of both benefit for oneself and others;
whereas the self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*) belongs exclusively to one's own benefit.
If the Enjoyment Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and the Emanation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*) pertain solely to the benefit of others because they manifest for the sake of others,
then the Essential Body (*svābhāvikakāya*) abides in the Dharma-nature Realm (*dharmatā-dhātu*).
Although there is no difference in essence between this body and its land,
they belong to the Buddha-dharma because their nature and characteristics are distinct.
This Buddha’s body and land are both not comprised within the category of form (*rūpa*).
Although their dimensions— whether small or large— cannot be described,
according to their phenomenal characteristics, their magnitude is boundless.
Just as space pervades all places,
the body of self-enjoyment likewise relies upon its own land;
that is to say, it is the pure consciousness associated with the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*).
Due to the maturation of the causes and conditions for a self-benefiting, untainted, and purely pure buddha-field cultivated in the past,
from the initial attainment of buddhahood until the end of the future,
he continuously transforms [the realm] into a purely pure buddha-field.
It is circular and boundless, adorned with various jewels,
and the Body of Self-Enjoyment constantly dwells therein;
its dimensions are equal to those of the Pure Land.
Each of the primary marks and secondary signs is boundless,
for they are produced by the guidance of infinite roots of goodness;
since merit and wisdom are not material phenomena (rūpa-dharma), [they cannot be measured].
Although its size or dimensions cannot be described,
it may nevertheless be said to pervade all places in terms of what is realized and the body upon which it relies;
the Body for Others' Enjoyment likewise relies upon its own land.
This refers to the power of the wisdom of equality and great compassion.
Through the ripening of the causes and conditions for purifying the Buddha-field— cultivated through past practice for the benefit of others—
it is transformed into a pure land according to what is appropriate for Bodhisattvas dwelling on the ten stages.
Whether small or large, inferior or superior, and subject to change over time,
the Enjoyment Body for Others (parasaṃbhogakāya) abides in dependence upon this; thus,
the dimensions of the supporting body are likewise not fixed.
If the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) relies upon a transformation land (nirmāṇabhūmi)— that is,
through the power of the wisdom of accomplishing activities (kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna) and great compassion—
then, due to the maturation of the causes and conditions for pure and impure Buddha-lands cultivated in the past for the benefit of others, [it manifests].
According to the suitability of sentient beings who have not yet ascended to the stages (*bhūmi*), he transforms it into a buddha-field—
whether pure or impure, small or large— and these undergo successive changes;
the Buddha’s transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) dwells in reliance upon it.
The dimensions of the bodies upon which they depend are likewise not fixed,
for the self-nature body and its land are realized identically by all Tathāgatas; thus,
in essence, there is no distinction between them.
Although the bodies of self-enjoyment and their supporting lands differ in their manifestations for each Buddha,
they are all infinite and do not obstruct one another.
As for the other two bodies and their lands, they are either common or uncommon depending on the sentient beings to be converted by each Tathāgata.
Regarding those who are transformed together, being in the same place at the same time,
the various Buddhas each manifest transformations into bodies and lands;
their forms are similar yet do not obstruct one another.
Interacting and mutually conditioning as dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*),
they cause the consciousnesses of those to be transformed to manifest their own perceptions;
that is to say, within a single land, there is a single Buddha-body.
He manifests supernatural powers and teaches the Dharma for their benefit.
Regarding those who are unique, there is only one Buddha’s transformation.
This is because, from beginningless time, the spiritual lineages (*gotra*) of all sentient beings have been naturally and inherently interconnected.
Either many belong to one,
or one belongs to many; therefore,
among those beings to be converted, there are both common and uncommon [objects].
Otherwise, it would be truly useless for many Buddhas to remain in the world for a long time,
each undergoing such arduous toil;
a single Buddha is capable of benefiting all sentient beings.
These various bodies and lands, whether pure or defiled, which are manifested upon the uncontaminated consciousness,
are identical in nature to the transforming consciousness itself— being wholesome and uncontaminated—
and are produced by purely wholesome and uncontaminated causes and conditions.
This is subsumed under the Truth of the Path,
as it is neither suffering nor its origin.
The characteristics of consciousness regarding the aggregates and so forth are not necessarily identical.
Because they are drawn forth through the intermingling of the causal conditions of the three dharmas,
those things manifested upon the outflow-tainted consciousness (sāsrava-vijñāna) are identical to the transforming consciousness itself;
all of them are outflow-tainted.
That which arises solely from impure causes and conditions is subsumed under the origin of suffering (*duḥkhasamudaya*),
because it is neither cessation (*nirodha*) nor the path (*mārga*).
The characteristics of wholesome and other types of consciousness are not necessarily identical.
Because the three natures are produced through a mixture of causes and conditions,
one should understand that the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth are likewise of both similar and dissimilar types.
However, that which is manifested is the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of consciousness.
Because they arise dependently,
their emptiness or reality is like that of consciousness;
the term "only" (vijñaptimātra) excludes external objects but does not negate internal objects.
If that were not so, then true suchness (tathatā) would likewise not be real.
Since internal objects and the aggregate of consciousness are neither false,
why do you say that there is only consciousness and no objects?
Consciousness exists only internally,
whereas its objects extend to both the internal and external;
[the author] fears confusion between them.
External objects are said to be mere consciousness.
Furthermore, all foolish worldlings, deludedly clinging to external objects, give rise to afflictions and karma, sinking into the cycle of birth and death;
they do not understand how to contemplate the mind and diligently seek liberation.
Out of compassion for them, he spoke the term "consciousness-only" (vijñaptimātra) so that they might observe their own minds and attain liberation from birth and death;
it does not mean that internal consciousness is entirely non-existent like external objects.
